biomes.name: Willow Meadow
biomes.description: A once-flowering meadow beside your home, now dusty and quiet. Native grasses were stripped away and the pollinators left with them.
biomes.restorationGoal: Replant grasses and wildflowers, add water and shelter, and help 10 meadow animals return.

biomes.name: Old Hollow Forest
biomes.description: A logged-over woodland. The big trees are gone, the understory is bare, and the birds have moved on.
biomes.restorationGoal: Rebuild the understory, raise nesting trees and deadwood, and welcome the forest animals back.

unlock.label: Restore Willow Meadow to 60% health, welcome 10 meadow animals, and craft a Forest Restoration Kit.

biomes.name: Rushwater Wetland
biomes.description: A drained marsh. Old channels are dry, the reeds are gone, and the water that remains is murky.
biomes.restorationGoal: Restore shallow water, reed beds, and mud banks so wetland life can return.

unlock.label: Restore Old Hollow Forest to 80% health with 10 forest animals back, welcome 25 animals across the whole preserve, and craft a Wetland Restoration Kit.

biomes.name: Redstone Scrubland
biomes.description: An overgrazed desert flat. Without brush or burrows, the heat keeps everything away.
biomes.restorationGoal: Replant cactus and brush, build shade and burrows, and bring the desert back to life.

unlock.label: Restore Rushwater Wetland to 80% health with 13 wetland animals back, welcome 45 animals across the whole preserve, and craft a Scrubland Restoration Kit.

biomes.name: Graywind Heights
biomes.description: A trampled alpine slope. The wildflower turf is worn through and the talus is silent.
biomes.restorationGoal: Restore alpine turf, snowmelt pools, and rocky shelter for high-country animals.

unlock.label: Restore Redstone Scrubland to 80% health with 15 desert animals back, welcome 65 animals across the whole preserve, and craft an Alpine Restoration Kit.

biomes.name: Pelican Shore
biomes.description: A scoured stretch of coast where the open ocean breaks along the western edge. The dunes have washed out and the tidepools are empty, but sea glass, kelp, coral, and the odd pearl still wash up on the tide.
biomes.restorationGoal: Anchor the dunes, restore tidepools and kelp wrack, and reopen the shore to coastal life.

unlock.label: Restore Graywind Heights to 80% health with 17 alpine animals back, welcome 85 animals across the whole preserve, and craft a Migration Path Marker.

animals.name: Banana Slug
animals.diet: fallen leaves, mushrooms, animal droppings and other decaying matter; occasionally live seedlings
animals.shelter: Under logs and loose bark; seals itself into a mucus cocoon and waits out dry spells
animals.preferredHabitat: Cool, shaded forest floor that stays damp — deep leaf litter, mossy logs and seeps
animals.fact: Banana slug slime is a numbing agent — one lick and most animals spit the slug straight back out, tongue tingling.
animals.role: The banana slug is the forest floor's shredder. Fungi and bacteria do the fine chemistry; the slug does the chewing, grinding fallen leaves into wet crumbs that rot far faster and turning a whole autumn of leaves into soft duff. It grazes mushrooms too, and spores ride safely through its gut, so every silver trail plants fungi somewhere new. Gartersnakes and raccoons are two of the very few animals willing to put up with the slime.

requirements.hint: Deep damp leaves, mossy shade and mushrooms to graze. Skip the pond — this one drinks through its skin, straight out of the litter.

animals.name: Tree Squirrel
animals.diet: acorns, hickory nuts, tree buds, samaras and fungi; occasional insects and bird eggs
animals.shelter: Tree cavity dens in winter and leaf-and-twig dreys built high in the canopy in summer
animals.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous or mixed forest rich in oaks and hickories
animals.fact: A squirrel buries thousands of nuts a year and forgets a good share of them. The forgotten ones grow into trees, so most squirrels accidentally plant a forest in a lifetime.
animals.role: The gray squirrel is a seed eater who keeps failing at his own plan, and the woods are better for it: acorns buried and never dug up again are how oaks climb hills and fill gaps. Its droppings scatter fungal spores, its leafy summer dreys get taken over by great horned owls, and being the commonest mid-sized animal in the forest it is on the menu of nearly every predator here.

requirements.hint: Oaks to feed and bury from, a high fork for a summer drey, and a big tree to den in over winter.

sources.name: NC Wildlife Resources Commission — Eastern Gray Squirrel

animals.name: Chipmunk
animals.diet: seeds, acorns, hickory nuts, berries and underground fungi, plus some insects and bird eggs
animals.shelter: Underground burrows up to 10 m long with a nest chamber and a seed-storage larder
animals.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous forest with logs, stumps and diggable soil
animals.fact: A chipmunk can cram so many acorns into its cheek pouches that its head looks twice as wide, then unload them into an underground pantry holding more than a litre of seeds. It wakes up all winter to snack — chipmunks never truly hibernate.
animals.role: The chipmunk is a hoarder and a digger. Every seed it carries off and never eats is a seed planted somewhere new, and spores from the fungi it digs up travel with it. Its tunnels loosen and air the soil. Small, common and awake in daylight, it is the prey base almost every predator here is waiting on — which is why so many of them cannot come back until it does.

requirements.hint: A brush pile to bolt into is enough to start with.

animals.name: Porcupine
animals.diet: almost entirely herbivorous — inner bark in winter, buds, twigs and leaves in summer — but gnaws shed antlers and bones for minerals
animals.shelter: Rock dens and hollow logs, reused season after season; also rests high in tree canopies
animals.preferredHabitat: Mixed and coniferous forest with thick-barked trees, especially hemlock, and rock or log dens below
animals.fact: A porcupine cannot throw its quills — they simply stick to whatever bumps them. The barbed tips are coated in a natural antibiotic, so a porcupine that falls out of a tree and lands on itself usually heals up fine.
animals.role: Porcupines improve the forest by damaging it. Stripping bark kills limbs and whole trees, and those dying trees become the snags, loose bark slabs and cavities that woodpeckers, bats and denning mammals move into — one animal's dinner is another animal's house. They eat the same nuts as squirrels and elk, and they are the entire reason a fisher would bother living here.

requirements.hint: Hemlock and pine bark to live on through winter, and a hollow log or rock den to sleep the day away in.

animals.name: Woodpecker
animals.diet: mostly insects — beetle larvae, ants, caterpillars — with some berries and sap
animals.shelter: Excavates its own cavity in a small dead stub, usually in wood already softened by fungus; roosts in cavities year-round
animals.preferredHabitat: Open deciduous and mixed woodland with small dead stubs and dead limbs on living trees
animals.fact: A downy woodpecker weighs about as much as four sheets of paper — light enough to hang off a dead weed stem and drill into it, which no bigger woodpecker can manage.
animals.role: The downy cuts the small holes. It can only chisel wood that fungi have already softened, so it waits on the decomposers — and the nuthatches and chickadees, which cannot cut a hole at all, wait on it. It works bark crevices and dead twigs for beetle grubs and ants that heavier woodpeckers can't reach, and its eggs feed climbing snakes.

requirements.hint: Small dead stubs with the wood already gone soft. It cannot chisel healthy timber, so leave the rotting stuff standing.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Downy Woodpecker life history

animals.name: Nuthatch
animals.diet: insects and spiders from bark in summer; acorns, hickory nuts and cached seeds through winter
animals.shelter: Natural cavities and old woodpecker holes in mature hardwoods; cannot excavate its own
animals.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous and mixed forest with large oaks and hickories
animals.fact: A nuthatch walks down tree trunks head-first, which lets it spot insects tucked in bark that every upward-climbing bird walks straight past.
animals.role: The nuthatch reads the bark upside down, taking beetles, insect eggs and spiders from angles other birds never see. In autumn it wedges acorns and seeds into bark cracks to hammer open later, shifting seed around the woods. It cannot cut a hole of its own, so it moves into last year's downy woodpecker hole — no woodpecker, no nuthatch.

requirements.hint: An old woodpecker hole it can move straight into, with big oaks to work over and stash seeds in.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — White-breasted Nuthatch

animals.name: Forest Salamander
animals.diet: small invertebrates: mites, springtails, spiders, beetles, ants and earthworms
animals.shelter: Under logs, bark and damp leaf litter; lays its eggs in a cavity inside rotting wood and stays coiled around them
animals.preferredHabitat: Cool, damp deciduous forest floor with abundant rotting wood — and no pond required anywhere in its life
animals.fact: Add up all the red-backed salamanders in a patch of forest and they can outweigh every bird in it. They have no lungs at all — the whole animal breathes through its skin.
animals.role: This salamander is the bridge between the leaf litter and everything above it: it eats the mites, springtails and small worms that shred fallen leaves, and its own huge numbers feed snakes, birds and small mammals. It also breaks the rule everyone learns about amphibians — no pond, no tadpole, the entire life cycle inside one rotting log. Skin-breathing means it dries out fast, so the ground has to stay damp.

requirements.hint: This one skips the tadpole stage completely — the eggs hatch fully formed inside a rotting log. No pond needed, just damp wood and deep leaves.

sources.name: Virginia Herpetological Society — Eastern Red-backed Salamander

animals.name: Raccoon
animals.diet: opportunistic: crayfish, insects, earthworms, frogs, eggs and fruit, with vertebrate prey a smaller share than most people assume
animals.shelter: Hollow tree dens preferred; also rock crevices, burrows and buildings
animals.preferredHabitat: Moist forest beside water shallow enough to wade and feel around in
animals.fact: A raccoon sees with its hands. Its front paws carry four to five times more touch nerves than most mammals', and it will stare off in the opposite direction while its fingers read a stream bed.
animals.role: The raccoon carries the stream into the woods: it feels out crayfish and insects in the shallows and unloads that energy up the bank, dropping fruit seeds as it goes. It is also this forest's great nest robber — the same crowd of cavities that lets wood ducks and flying squirrels move in hands a raccoon a list of doors to try.

requirements.hint: A hollow den log and a stony shallow edge to feel around in. It hunts with its hands, not its eyes.

animals.name: Black Bear
animals.diet: berries, acorns and nuts above all; also grasses and forbs, insects and grubs, carrion, and fawns in spring
animals.shelter: Winter dens under upturned root masses, in hollow trees and rock cavities, or dug into a bank
animals.preferredHabitat: Dense forest with a thick understory and reliable berry and acorn crops
animals.fact: Black bear cubs are born in the middle of hibernation, blind and smaller than a soup can, and their mother barely wakes up for it.
animals.role: A black bear ties the whole forest together in one animal: berries, acorns, grubs torn out of rotting logs, an elk calf in spring. It carries berry seeds for miles before dropping them, and every log it rips apart rots faster afterwards. A bear's year is really an acorn year — when the mast crop fails bears wander enormous distances, and a forest with no oaks cannot keep them. Nothing here hunts a grown bear.

requirements.hint: A full larder and a winter bed: heavy berry crops, acorn-bearing oaks, water, and a den under the tipped-up roots of a fallen tree.

animals.name: Gray Fox
animals.diet: mice, voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds and eggs — and in late summer an astonishing amount of fruit
animals.shelter: Hollow logs, rock crevices and old earth dens; it will also curl up on a branch well off the ground
animals.preferredHabitat: Brushy woodland edges and old clearings growing back, with tangled climbable cover
animals.fact: It is the only dog in the world that climbs trees. A gray fox hooks its curved claws into the bark, shins up the trunk like a cat, and naps ten metres up where nothing that hunts it can follow.
animals.role: The forest's climbing fox. It works the brushy edges for mice, rabbits and ground-nesting birds, then goes straight up a trunk after squirrels, nests and grapes. By late summer it is eating so much fruit that its droppings are half seeds, which plants the next generation of berry tangles all along the edge. Bobcats kill it when they catch it in the open and great horned owls take its kits, so it keeps a climbable tree within a sprint at all times.

requirements.hint: A brushy edge to hunt along, a dry bank to den in, and something woody to climb — going straight up a trunk is how this one gets away from whatever is bigger. Fruit matters as much as mice here.

animals.name: Ratsnake
animals.diet: mice, voles, chipmunks and young squirrels, plus birds and eggs lifted straight out of nests
animals.shelter: Hollow trunks, rot pockets and stump cavities; the eggs go into a warm heap of rotting wood chips
animals.preferredHabitat: Old woods and woodland edges with big rough-barked trees to climb and rodents underneath them
animals.fact: A ratsnake can climb straight up a bare tree trunk with nothing to hold onto. It wedges the edges of its belly scales into the ridges in the bark and walks up the side of the tree, then robs the nest at the top.
animals.role: The forest's rodent brake, and the only hunter here that works in three dimensions. On the ground it takes mice, voles and chipmunks by the dozen; up in the canopy it raids old woodpecker holes and songbird nests, which is why every bird in earshot mobs it. It kills by wrapping and squeezing, not venom, and when it is startled it freezes into a stiff kinked shape that looks exactly like a fallen branch. She never sits on her eggs — she buries them in rotting wood and lets the heat of the rot do the incubating. Foxes, fishers and great horned owls eat it.

requirements.hint: Big rough-barked trees are the whole trick — this snake hunts up them as much as under them. Leave a heap of rotting wood chips at the foot of a stump for her eggs, and skip the pond; she does not need one.

animals.name: Bobcat
animals.diet: obligate carnivore: rabbits, squirrels and rodents, plus some birds, reptiles and deer fawns
animals.shelter: Dens under rock ledges, in hollow logs and in dense thickets; a female moves her kittens if disturbed
animals.preferredHabitat: Forest with a dense understory, brushy edges and broken rocky ground
animals.fact: A bobcat can bring down prey eight times its own weight, then bury the leftovers under leaves or snow and come back the next night.
animals.role: With no wolves or cougars in these woods, the bobcat is the top hunter on the ground and nothing hunts a grown one. It takes everything from chipmunks up to raccoons, foxes and even fishers, and it kills by ambush — creeping close through cover, then one short rush. Strip the understory and the bobcat leaves, however much prey is still standing around: it has nothing left to hide behind.

requirements.hint: Dense understory to stalk through, a sheltered rock den for kittens, and plenty of prey already back.

animals.name: Great Horned Owl
animals.diet: mammals and birds — rabbits, skunks, even other owls — plus frogs
animals.shelter: Never builds a nest: takes over an old hawk, crow or squirrel nest, or a broken snag top or ledge
animals.preferredHabitat: Mature forest broken by open ground, with big trees holding other animals' abandoned nests
animals.fact: Great horned owls are one of the only animals that regularly kill and eat skunks. The spray does not appear to bother them in the slightest.
animals.role: The great horned owl runs the night shift and eats a longer list of animals than any other bird of prey here — squirrels, bats, snakes, ducks, even porcupines — and adults have nothing above them. It builds nothing at all: it starts nesting in midwinter by claiming an old squirrel drey or hawk nest somebody else made last spring, which is why the squirrels have to come back before the owl can.

requirements.hint: Tall trees holding somebody else's old nest — this one never builds its own — and prey already back in the woods.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Great Horned Owl life history

animals.name: Grasshopper
animals.diet: grasses, sedges and broadleaf forbs
animals.shelter: Shelters down in grass and low vegetation; lays eggs in firm bare soil
animals.preferredHabitat: Sunny grasslands and meadows rich in grasses and forbs
animals.fact: A grasshopper's ears are on its belly — a pair of eardrums on the first segment of the abdomen, nowhere near its head.
animals.role: Grasshoppers turn grass into food for everything else. Almost every meat-eater in this meadow takes them at some point — birds, snakes, foxes, spiders, mantises, even a screech owl — so a good grasshopper summer is a good summer for the whole food web.

requirements.hint: They return almost as soon as the grass does.

animals.name: Prairie Vole
animals.diet: grasses, sedges, seeds and roots, plus bark in winter
animals.shelter: Shallow burrows and woven grass nests linked by clipped surface runways
animals.preferredHabitat: Dense grassy prairie and meadow with thick ground cover left standing
animals.fact: Prairie voles pair up and stay together, and both parents raise the pups — which is why scientists who study bonding and loyalty end up studying this small brown rodent.
animals.role: The vole is the meadow's engine of small furry food. It mows narrow highways through the grass, breeds fast, and feeds hawks, owls, foxes, coyotes, snakes and badgers. The burrows it abandons get taken over by bumble bee queens and garter snakes, so it builds homes as well as filling stomachs.

requirements.hint: Thick unmown grass with clipped runways beneath it. This one arrives early, and almost everything with teeth or talons is waiting on it.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Microtus ochrogaster

animals.name: Monarch Butterfly
animals.diet: caterpillars eat only milkweed; adults sip flower nectar
animals.shelter: Roosts in trees and shrubs; overwinters clustered in dense groves far to the south
animals.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and roadsides with milkweed to breed on and nectar flowers to refuel on
animals.fact: No single monarch flies the whole round trip. The butterflies that head south in autumn are the great-grandchildren of the ones that came north in spring, and they find the same groves anyway.
animals.role: Monarch caterpillars eat milkweed and store its poison in their own bodies, so a bird that tries one usually spits it out and remembers the orange for the rest of its life. It doesn't save them from everything — mantises, spiders, wasps and ants take eggs and caterpillars by the thousand, and only a few in every hundred ever grow wings.

requirements.hint: A spreading milkweed bed for the caterpillars — nothing else will do — and nectar flowers close by for the adults.

animals.name: Bumblebee
animals.diet: nectar for fuel and pollen for protein, from a wide range of flowers
animals.shelter: Nests in abandoned rodent burrows, grass tussocks and ground cavities
animals.preferredHabitat: Flower-rich meadows with something in bloom from spring to frost
animals.fact: Some flowers refuse to let go of their pollen unless they are shaken. A bumblebee grabs on and buzzes its flight muscles until the pollen falls out — tomatoes and blueberries depend on it.
animals.role: Big, furry and warm enough to fly on cold grey mornings when other bees are still grounded, the bumblebee is the meadow's heavy-duty pollinator. A whole colony starts with one queen in spring hunting for an old vole hole to move into, so nest holes matter every bit as much as flowers. Orb weavers and crab spiders take her at the flowers, and badgers dig entire nests out of the ground.

requirements.hint: Flowers are only half of it. A queen also needs an abandoned vole hole under a thick grass tussock to start her colony in.

animals.name: Cottontail Rabbit
animals.diet: grasses and clover in summer; twigs, bark and buds in winter
animals.shelter: Rests in shallow grass 'forms'; bolts into brush piles and old burrows
animals.preferredHabitat: Meadows and field edges with brushy cover close enough to run to
animals.fact: A cottontail doesn't dig a burrow. It presses a shallow bowl into the grass called a form and sits so still in it that you can walk straight past.
animals.role: Cottontails eat grass and clover all summer and switch to twigs and bark in winter, and they breed fast enough to keep up with everything that hunts them — fox, coyote, badger, hawk and owl all count on them. Their droppings feed the soil life underfoot, which is a polite way of saying rabbits fertilise the meadow they eat.

requirements.hint: A brushy form to bolt into, native grass to graze, and berries close by. It gets most of its water straight out of green plants.

animals.name: Mule Deer
animals.diet: shrubs, forbs, twigs and buds, plus grasses in spring
animals.shelter: Beds down in brushy cover or tall grass; no permanent den
animals.preferredHabitat: Open meadows and shrubby edges with browse and daily water
animals.fact: A bounding mule deer lands on all four hooves at once like a pogo stick, and puffs out scent from a gland on its hind leg as it goes — a warning the other deer can smell.
animals.role: The mule deer is a browser rather than a grazer: it works on shrub twigs, buds and broad-leaved plants instead of cropping turf, so it shapes the edges of the meadow rather than the middle. Its browsing and droppings move nutrients around. Coyotes take fawns; a healthy adult is more than most hunters here want to take on.

requirements.hint: Real browse — serviceberry twigs and buds, not lawn — plus water it can reach every day.

animals.name: Ladybug
animals.diet: aphids and other small soft-bodied insects, as both larva and adult
animals.shelter: Overwinters packed into leaf litter in big huddles; shelters on foliage in summer
animals.preferredHabitat: Meadows with aphid-bearing plants, especially milkweed
animals.fact: One ladybug can put away around 5,000 aphids in a lifetime. Pinch it and it bleeds bitter yellow blood out of its knees, which is why most birds spit it straight back out.
animals.role: Larva and adult both hunt aphids, so a ladybug's whole life runs on an aphid supply — in this meadow, the yellow oleander aphids crowding the milkweed stems. Its bright shell is a warning label and it works on most birds. Mantises and orb weavers are not most birds.

requirements.hint: A patch of clover. The aphids arrive on their own, and that is the whole invitation.

animals.name: Ground Squirrel
animals.diet: mostly seeds, grasses, flowers and fungi, plus insects like grasshoppers
animals.shelter: Big multi-entrance burrow systems dug into deep open ground
animals.preferredHabitat: Open grassy meadow and slopes with a stone wall or bank to keep watch from
animals.fact: Facing a rattlesnake, this squirrel kicks sand and waves its tail — and pumps hot blood into the tail first, so the snake's heat-sensing pits see a far bigger animal than is really standing there.
animals.role: A digger and a generalist. It eats seeds, greens, fungi and insects, turns over soil every time it excavates, and the tunnels it abandons become homes for bumble bee queens, garter snakes and foxes. Its colonies are what pull badgers, hawks and coyotes into a meadow in the first place.

requirements.hint: Deep diggable soil for a burrow town, and a stone wall to stand sentry on.

sources.name: PNAS — infrared tail-flagging in ground squirrels

animals.name: Western Meadowlark
animals.diet: mostly insects in summer — beetles, grasshoppers, crickets — and seeds in winter
animals.shelter: A domed grass nest woven on the ground, usually with a covered runway leading in
animals.preferredHabitat: Wide native grassland with song perches and no shrubs moving in
animals.fact: A meadowlark weaves a roof over its nest and a covered tunnel leading in, so from above there is nothing to see at all — just grass.
animals.role: A grassland bird through and through. It eats grasshoppers, crickets and beetles by the hundred all summer and switches to seed in winter, and it needs real open space — as shrubs and trees creep in, meadowlarks quietly vanish. A plump bird that nests on the ground is a favourite of hawks, foxes, badgers and coyotes.

requirements.hint: Wide unbroken native grass and a perch to sing from. Skip the shrubs here — woody cover is exactly what pushes this one out.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Western Meadowlark

animals.name: Garter Snake
animals.diet: earthworms, pillbugs, amphibians, slugs, insects and young rodents
animals.shelter: Shelters under stone walls and logs; winters below the frost line in a communal den
animals.preferredHabitat: Moist meadow and grassland near sunny stones and water
animals.fact: Garter snakes spend the whole winter piled together by the dozen in one frost-free hole underground, and come pouring back out of it in a knot in spring.
animals.role: The meadow's damp-grass hunter — earthworms, pillbugs, frogs, insects and young voles, always within reach of water. It is harmless to people, though a bite can itch. Where it can survive the winter is what decides where it can live at all, so one deep frost-free den matters more than anything else you can build for it.

requirements.hint: Water to hunt beside, warm stone to bask on, and a den deep enough to spend the winter below the frost.

animals.name: Red Fox
animals.diet: voles, rabbits, squirrels, birds and insects, rounded out with berries and carrion
animals.shelter: Enlarges a burrow another animal dug into a natal den; also uses brush and hollows
animals.preferredHabitat: Meadows, field edges and hedgerows across open country
animals.fact: A fox listening for a vole under deep grass or snow lines itself up facing magnetic north before it leaps — and the trick only seems to help when it cannot see the prey at all.
animals.role: A stalk-and-pounce generalist that keeps rodent and rabbit numbers down and fills the gaps with insects, berries and whatever it finds already dead. It rarely digs a den from scratch — it widens an old ground squirrel or badger burrow instead. Great horned owls take its kits, and now that coyotes are back, foxes have to give ground.

requirements.hint: This one comes back once the small animals do — and she needs an old burrow she can widen into a nursery.

sources.name: Phys.org — magnetic alignment in fox predation (Cerveny et al.)

animals.name: Red-tailed Hawk
animals.diet: mostly small mammals — voles, ground squirrels, rabbits — plus birds and snakes
animals.shelter: A bulky stick nest in the crown of a tall tree or on a cliff ledge
animals.preferredHabitat: Open country seen from above: grassland, fields and meadows
animals.fact: That screaming eagle cry in every film is a red-tailed hawk. Actual bald eagles sound like squeaky gulls, so the movies quietly swapped them.
animals.role: The daylight hunter over this meadow, either circling on broad flat wings or sitting on a pole staring at the grass. It is heavy and powerful and built for taking prey off the ground — voles, ground squirrels, rabbits, snakes — not for chasing birds through the air. The huge stick nest it builds gets inherited by a great horned owl the very next winter.

requirements.hint: A tall tree crown for the stick nest, open grass to hunt over, and a meadow already full of small mammals. It takes its water from its prey.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Red-tailed Hawk

animals.name: Minnow
animals.diet: algae, diatoms and plankton sifted off mud, stems and stones, plus detritus and small insect larvae.
animals.shelter: Reed roots, submerged plant beds, and the shaded underside of sunken wood.
animals.preferredHabitat: Connected, clean, weedy pools.
animals.fact: The male minnow scrubs the underside of a sunken slab spotless using a spongy pad on his own back, then guards the eggs the females glue to that ceiling — fanning them day and night until they hatch.
animals.role: The little silver engine of the marsh. Minnow schools graze algae and plankton and then get eaten by nearly everything with a bill, a beak or a claw — and they give baby mussels a free ride to new water on their gills.

requirements.hint: Clean pools that join up to each other, plus something flat and submerged for the males to glue their eggs underneath.

sources.name: Missouri Department of Conservation — Fathead Minnow

animals.name: Beaver
animals.diet: bark and cambium of willow and aspen, plus cattail rhizomes and submerged plants
animals.shelter: Stick-and-mud lodges with underwater entrances
animals.preferredHabitat: Slow channels with mud banks and woody plants to fell
animals.fact: A beaver's front teeth never stop growing and are orange because they are reinforced with iron — living chisels that gnawing keeps sharp. Its lips shut behind those teeth, so it can carry and cut branches underwater without swallowing the pond.
animals.role: The marsh's engineer, and the turning point of the whole restoration. Fell a few willows, dam a channel, and suddenly there is deep permanent water with drowned trees standing in it — the pond the otter, the merganser, the kingfisher, the heron and the eagle all move in on afterwards.

requirements.hint: Willows to fell and eat, a soft bank to den in, and enough water to float a log. Once it settles, seven new habitats become buildable.

sources.name: US Forest Service — Beaver as ecosystem engineers

animals.name: Muskrat
animals.diet: mainly cattails, bulrush and roots; sometimes freshwater mussels and small fish
animals.shelter: Dome lodges woven from cattail and reed, and burrows dug into banks
animals.preferredHabitat: Reedy shallows with abundant cattails
animals.fact: A muskrat can stay under for a quarter of an hour on one breath, and in midwinter it dives beneath the ice to dig up frozen-in cattail roots and eat them down there in the dark.
animals.role: The cattail harvester. It clips reeds into lodges and feeding lanes that ducks and herons then hunt along, it feeds the mink, the otter and the eagle, and the bank burrows it abandons are the only homes mink ever move into.

requirements.hint: Cattails to eat and to build lodges from, and shallow water over their roots so it can keep feeding all winter.

animals.name: Mallard
animals.diet: mostly seeds and submerged plants, though hens switch to insect larvae, snails and freshwater shrimp while laying, and ducklings eat almost nothing else at first
animals.shelter: Ground nests hidden in dense sedge and grass tussocks near water
animals.preferredHabitat: Calm, plant-rich shallows with tussock cover on the bank
animals.fact: Mallards sleep with one eye open and half the brain awake. On a raft of sleeping ducks it is the ones on the outside doing the watching — and they swap places so everyone gets a proper nap.
animals.role: The tail-up dabbler of the shallows, tipping forward to reach seeds and leaves it can't dive for. Hens switch to insects and snails while they are laying, and ducklings eat almost nothing else at first, so a mallard family needs a bug-rich marsh, not just a weedy one.

requirements.hint: Water shallow enough to tip into headfirst, and thick dry tussocks a few steps up the bank for the hen to hide her nest in.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Mallard life history

animals.name: Painted Turtle
animals.diet: mostly aquatic plants and algae as an adult; hatchlings and young turtles eat far more insects and carrion
animals.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; hauls out onto logs to bask
animals.preferredHabitat: Still water with basking logs
animals.fact: A painted turtle spends the entire winter under the ice without taking a breath. It absorbs what oxygen it can through its back end, and when that runs short it dissolves minerals out of its own shell to stay alive until spring.
animals.role: The marsh's sunbather. A cold turtle cannot digest a thing, so a log in the sun is a feeding requirement rather than a luxury — and as painted turtles grow they flip from hunting insects to grazing plants.

requirements.hint: Still water, a soft mud bottom, and a log tilted up out of the water. No sunny log, no digestion.

sources.name: Turtle Guardians — Butt breathers and frogsicles: overwintering herpetofauna

animals.name: Red-winged Blackbird
animals.diet: insects in summer, seeds and grain the rest of the year
animals.shelter: Cup nests wound around several upright stems standing in water
animals.preferredHabitat: Dense cattail and reed stands with water underneath
animals.fact: A male red-wing can switch his scarlet shoulder patches on and off. Flared wide they start fights; tucked away under the black feathers they let him slip through a rival's territory completely unnoticed.
animals.role: The loudest bird in the marsh and the first one back in spring. It hunts insects all summer and switches to seeds for the rest of the year, and it winds its nest around standing stems with water underneath — a moat the mink will not cross.

requirements.hint: Standing stems with water beneath them. The nest is stitched around the reeds and the water underneath is the burglar alarm.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Red-winged Blackbird life history

animals.name: Sandhill Crane
animals.diet: grains, tubers, insects, crayfish and small animals
animals.shelter: Large ground mounds of piled marsh plants standing in shallow water
animals.preferredHabitat: Broad, quiet, restored marshland
animals.fact: Cranes dance to choose a partner — leaping, bowing and flinging sticks in the air — and once they pair up they usually stay together for life. Their bugling carries more than two kilometres because the windpipe is coiled up inside the breastbone like a trumpet.
animals.role: The tallest bird on the marsh and the last one to arrive. Cranes probe the mud for tubers and snap up frogs, crayfish and insects, and they will only settle where the water is wide, quiet and genuinely healthy.

requirements.hint: This one wants space and quiet. Build a wide, well-balanced marsh and heap a nest mound up above the waterline.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Sandhill Crane life history

animals.name: Chorus Frog
animals.diet: small insects and other tiny invertebrates
animals.shelter: Damp litter and loose bark under fallen wood in winter; wet vegetation in summer
animals.preferredHabitat: Shallow pools ringed with reeds and wet meadow
animals.fact: A chorus frog freezes solid every winter. Ice fills the spaces around its organs, its heart stops for weeks — and in spring it thaws out and starts singing as though nothing happened. The call sounds exactly like running your thumb along a comb.
animals.role: Small enough to sit on a coin and loud enough to hear right across the marsh. It mops up tiny insects all summer and then feeds herons, mink, otters and cranes — the most-eaten voice in the wetland.

requirements.hint: Shallow water to sing and breed in, and a deep, damp pile of leaves on dry land to spend the winter frozen inside.

sources.name: Michigan Natural Features Inventory — Pseudacris maculata
Montana Field Guide — Boreal Chorus Frog

animals.name: Tiger Salamander
animals.diet: worms, insects, freshwater shrimp and other small invertebrates; larvae take tadpoles
animals.shelter: Damp burrows in soft ground near fishless breeding pools
animals.preferredHabitat: Fishless seasonal pools with soft banks
animals.fact: Tiger salamanders spend most of their lives alone underground, then walk back on the first warm rainy night of spring to the exact pool they hatched in — and if that pool starts drying too fast, some larvae grow oversized heads and start eating their own brothers and sisters.
animals.role: A fat, blotched, black-and-gold hunter that only breeds where fish cannot live. Its larvae race to grow legs before the pool dries, which is a bet they can only win in water no minnow could survive.

requirements.hint: Dig the vernal pools well away from the fish pools and let them dry right out in summer. Fish and it larvae cannot share water.

sources.name: US Fish & Wildlife Service — Eastern Tiger Salamander

animals.name: Dragonfly
animals.diet: flying insects as an adult; the underwater nymph takes midge larvae, freshwater shrimp, tadpoles and fish fry
animals.shelter: Emergent reed stems for the adults; the nymphs live in the water below
animals.preferredHabitat: Clean open water with emergent stems to climb out on
animals.fact: Dragonflies catch about 95 out of every 100 things they chase — a better strike rate than a lion, a shark or a falcon. They also see the world in something close to slow motion, which is why swatting one never works.
animals.role: A hunter with two completely different lives. The nymph spends a year underwater firing out a hinged, grabbing lower lip at tadpoles and fish fry; then it climbs a reed stem, splits its own back open and flies away to hunt mosquitoes over the marsh.

requirements.hint: Open, clean water for the nymphs below, and tall stems at the edge for them to climb when it is time to change.

sources.name: Natural History Museum — Dragonflies: the ultimate hunters

animals.name: Mink
animals.diet: fish, frogs, crayfish, muskrats, and the eggs and young of marsh birds
animals.shelter: Bank burrows, usually taken over from muskrats rather than dug
animals.preferredHabitat: Brushy banks beside busy water
animals.fact: A mink will chase a fish thirty metres underwater, and it hunts on land, in the water and up trees. What it almost never does is dig — it simply moves into a burrow a muskrat made and does not ask.
animals.role: A small brown fury with an enormous menu: fish, frogs, crayfish, muskrats, eggs, ducklings, whatever is slowest that day. Its home is always second-hand, so no muskrats usually means no mink no matter how much prey there is.

requirements.hint: Water to hunt in, and a bank den — but something else has to dig that den first.

animals.name: Great Blue Heron
animals.diet: fish, frogs, salamanders, crayfish and large insects
animals.shelter: Colonial stick nests built high in tall trees and snags near water
animals.preferredHabitat: Still shallows for slow, patient hunting, with tall nest trees within reach
animals.fact: A heron's neck has one specially kinked bone in it that works like a loaded spring — the strike is over faster than you can blink, and the fish is caught crosswise in the bill rather than speared.
animals.role: The tall grey statue of the shallows. It hunts alone but flatly refuses to nest alone, packing dozens of stick nests into one stand of tall trees — and it spends a good part of its life being chased and robbed of its catch by eagles.

requirements.hint: Shallow water full of fish and frogs, and a stand of tall trees for the colony. This one nests alongside its own kind or not at all.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Great Blue Heron life history
Audubon Field Guide — Great Blue Heron

animals.name: River Otter
animals.diet: fish, crayfish, mussels, frogs and other aquatic animals
animals.shelter: Bank dens with underwater entrances — usually a beaver's old lodge or burrow
animals.preferredHabitat: Clean, connected water rich in fish and slow prey
animals.fact: An otter has around 350,000 hairs packed into every square centimetre of its fur — more than most animals have on their entire body. It is the air trapped in all that fur, not fat, that keeps an otter warm in freezing water.
animals.role: The best swimmer in the marsh and the top hunter under the surface. Otters need a lot of clean connected water and a den they did not dig themselves, so an otter here means the beaver came back first — and it means the eagles finally have someone worth robbing.

requirements.hint: Lots of connected clean water, plenty of fish and crayfish, and an old beaver-made bank den with an underwater door.

animals.name: Snow Flea
animals.diet: dead leaves and stems, fungal threads, pollen, and the pink algae that grow on old snow
animals.shelter: Wet leaf litter, moss cushions, and the hollow gap between the snowpack and the ground in winter
animals.preferredHabitat: Damp alpine turf, moss cushions and snowmelt litter, plus the surface of late-lying snow on warm days
animals.fact: On a mild winter day snow fleas pour out onto the snow in their thousands, like somebody spilled pepper across the drift. Their blood is full of natural antifreeze, so they keep moving when everything else is frozen stiff.
animals.role: The clean-up crew, and the reason last year's leaves do not simply pile up forever. Snow fleas shred dead stems and graze fungal threads into soil, and they keep at it all winter in the dark gap between the snowpack and the ground. Pipits, finches, chickadees, bluebirds, nutcrackers and toads all snap them up.

requirements.hint: A mat of litter under melting snow is enough to start.

animals.name: Bighorn Sheep
animals.diet: chiefly grasses and sedges, with forbs and woody browse in winter
animals.shelter: Beds on rocky ledges and rugged escape terrain near cliffs
animals.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf directly beside steep, broken escape cliffs
animals.fact: Rams charge each other and crash horns hard enough to be heard a mile off. Their skulls are double-layered to take the hit, and a lamb is climbing rock within a day of being born.
animals.role: A cliff-edge grazer that crops turf on open slopes and never feeds further from broken rock than it can sprint. Mountain lions take adults and lambs, and eagles carry newborn lambs off the ledges.

requirements.hint: Good grazing is only half of it. It will not use a slope it cannot escape from, so put the turf right up against broken cliff — and a mineral lick nearby, because it will travel a long way for salt.

animals.name: Pika
animals.diet: grasses, forbs, wildflowers and lichen, cut green and dried into winter haypiles
animals.shelter: Cool gaps deep within talus and broken rock
animals.preferredHabitat: Deep, stable talus with alpine flower turf right at its edge
animals.fact: A pika spends its whole summer cutting flowers and grass and stacking them into little haystacks under the rocks, then eats its way through the pile in the dark under the snow.
animals.role: A hamster-shaped cousin of rabbits that lives in the gaps inside talus and squeaks at anything that comes near. It overheats after an hour of warm sun, so it works at dawn and dusk, and it has already vanished from the lower, hotter rockslides, which makes it the mountain's early warning system. Weasels, martens, foxes, wolverines and eagles all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Deep talus to vanish into with flowers a short dash away, then a haypile. Without cured hay it cannot last the winter.

animals.name: Yellow-bellied Marmot
animals.diet: grasses, flowering plants and seeds, eaten hard through a short summer
animals.shelter: Deep, many-chambered burrows dug beneath boulders, below the frost line
animals.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf broken by boulders, with diggable soil underneath
animals.fact: A yellow-bellied marmot sleeps for about eight months of the year and wakes up weighing half what it did when it went to bed.
animals.role: A fat, sun-basking rodent that eats meadow plants flat out through a short summer and whistles from a boulder the moment a shadow crosses. Its old burrows become fox dens, bumble bee nests and toad hideouts, so a surprising amount of the mountain depends on its digging. Eagles, foxes, martens, wolverines and lions hunt it.

requirements.hint: Soil deep enough to dig, a boulder to dig under, and a lot of green within waddling distance. Do not go looking after early autumn, because it is underground until spring.

animals.name: Snowshoe Hare
animals.diet: green plants in summer; willow and juniper twigs, buds, bark and conifer needles in winter
animals.shelter: Shallow 'forms' scraped under dense shrubs and low conifer branches
animals.preferredHabitat: Dense krummholz, juniper and willow thickets at and just below treeline
animals.fact: The hare changes colour by the calendar, not the weather. Shortening days flip its coat white whether the snow has turned up or not, so a warm autumn can leave a white hare sitting on brown ground.
animals.role: A browsing hare of thick treeline cover with back feet like snowshoes that hold it up on top of drifts. It freezes rather than runs, so tangled low cover is everything to it, and willow twigs get it through the winter. Martens, foxes, eagles, wolverines and lions all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Low tangled cover it can freeze motionless inside, a scraped hollow under the krummholz to sit out the day, and willow to browse in winter. Open ground with a rock pile on it is the opposite of what it wants. It eats snow instead of drinking.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Lepus americanus

animals.name: White-tailed Ptarmigan
animals.diet: buds, twigs, leaves, seeds and flowers; in winter almost entirely willow buds and twigs
animals.shelter: Camouflaged ground scrapes among lichen-covered rock, and burrows dug into soft snow to roost
animals.preferredHabitat: Alpine tundra above treeline year-round, dropping into sheltered willow basins in winter
animals.fact: It grows feathers on its feet for winter, built-in snowshoes, and then dives into a snowdrift to sleep, because inside the drift it is far warmer than out in the wind.
animals.role: A grouse that spends its entire life above the trees, mottled brown in summer and pure white in winter and so well hidden that people walk within a metre without seeing one. Willow buds are almost its whole winter diet. Eagles, foxes, weasels, martens and wolverines hunt it and its chicks.

requirements.hint: Willow is the whole winter for this one, and a soft deep drift is its bedroom. It eats snow instead of drinking, and it has no use at all for a flower planter.

sources.name: All About Birds — White-tailed Ptarmigan life history

animals.name: Alpine Butterfly
animals.diet: stonecrop as a caterpillar, then nectar from stonecrop and daisies as an adult
animals.shelter: No nest — the caterpillar develops fully inside the egg and overwinters there, hatching at snowmelt
animals.preferredHabitat: Rocky open alpine and subalpine slopes where stonecrop grows between the stones
animals.fact: Its wings are almost see-through, like waxed paper held up to the light, and the red spots are a warning. Birds that try one usually spit it straight back out.
animals.role: A butterfly that flies in air most insects cannot manage. Its caterpillars eat stonecrop and absolutely nothing else, so the butterfly only lives where the stonecrop does, while the adults drift between meadow flowers for nectar. Pipits and bluebirds still catch a few.

requirements.hint: Nectar keeps the adults hanging around. Stonecrop is what keeps them for good. Plant flowers without the caterpillar's one food plant and all you get is visitors.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Parnassius smintheus

animals.name: Alpine Moth
animals.diet: flower nectar as an adult, drunk after dark; leaves and roots down in the lowlands as a caterpillar
animals.shelter: Packed by the thousand into cracks under scree slabs, out of the sun and the wind
animals.preferredHabitat: High rockslides beside flower turf — but only in summer; it spends the rest of the year far below
animals.fact: Every summer millions of these moths fly up out of the lowlands and hide in the rock on the highest peaks. They are so fatty that a bear will spend all day flipping stones to eat them, and can put away forty thousand moths in a single day.
animals.role: The mountain's fuel delivery. The moths fatten on lowland flowers, then migrate hundreds of kilometres uphill to sit out the summer in the cold rock, and every one arrives as a little parcel of fat richer than anything else growing up here. Bears, birds and just about everything that hunts a rockslide feeds on them. At night they come out to drink nectar and pollinate high-country flowers; by dawn they are back under the slabs. Break up the loose rock and the whole larder goes with it.
eatsOther: leaves and roots as a caterpillar

requirements.hint: Flowers to drink from at night and loose slabs to hide under by day. It only shows up in high summer — the rest of the year it is a caterpillar a long way downhill.

sources.name: USGS Northern Rocky Mountain Science Center — Army Cutworm Moth Aggregation Sites

animals.name: Rock Squirrel
animals.diet: seeds, berries and green shoots, plus underground fungi, insects and the occasional egg
animals.shelter: A burrow driven in under a boulder or a fallen log, with a grass-lined sleeping chamber at the far end
animals.preferredHabitat: Sunny rocky slopes, talus edges and open dwarf-pine ground at and above the tree line
animals.fact: Everyone calls it a giant chipmunk, but look at its face — no stripes on the cheeks. And it does not just nap through winter: it cools until its body is barely above freezing and its heart slows to a few beats a minute.
animals.role: A stripe-backed seed machine that spends the short summer eating itself round, then vanishes underground for half the year. It buries seeds all over the slope and forgets enough of them to replant it, and it digs up and eats underground fungi, so the spores ride through its gut and get planted somewhere new. Ermines, martens, lynx and eagles all hunt it, and the tunnels it abandons become shelter for toads and beetles.

requirements.hint: It is only above ground for half the year, so look for it in the warm months. Seed-heavy flowers to fatten on, rock to duck into, and diggable ground under a boulder for the long sleep.

sources.name: Montana Field Guide — Golden-mantled Ground Squirrel

animals.name: Nutcracker
animals.diet: whitebark and limber pine seeds cached by the thousand, plus insects and small animals
animals.shelter: Cup nest in a conifer, sited near the winter seed caches
animals.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest and krummholz within reach of pine-seed sources
animals.fact: One bird buries tens of thousands of pine seeds in a single autumn and can still find them months later under snow, navigating by rocks and logs it has memorised like landmarks on a map.
animals.role: A crow-family bird with a deal running with the whitebark pine. The cones never open by themselves, so nearly every young whitebark on the mountain grew from a seed this bird buried and never came back for. It carries seeds in a pouch under its tongue, breeds in late winter off its hoard, and takes insects and small animals besides. Martens and eagles catch it.

requirements.hint: It needs a seed bank it can find again under the snow. Build the caches, and the pines it forgets to dig up become next year's forest.

sources.name: All About Birds — Clark's Nutcracker life history

animals.name: Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch
animals.diet: tiny alpine plant seeds and insects, often gleaned off the surface of snowfields
animals.shelter: Bulky cup of moss and grass wedged deep into a cliff crack or a hole in talus
animals.preferredHabitat: Above treeline: talus, scree, cliff faces and the edges of permanent snow
animals.fact: It nests higher than almost any other songbird here, jammed into cracks in cliffs and rockslides where nothing else will build at all.
animals.role: A pink-brown finch that hops across snowfields picking up wind-blown seeds and insects the cold has knocked flat. It can only breed where the rock has real cracks in it, so cliffs matter to it even more than food does. Eagles and ermines take it.

requirements.hint: Rock with cracks in it, not a heap of stones. This one nests inside the cliff, feeds out across the scree, and drinks meltwater.

sources.name: All About Birds — Gray-crowned Rosy-Finch life history

animals.name: Pipit
animals.diet: mostly insects, springtails, spiders and their larvae, plus some seeds
animals.shelter: Ground nest of grass tucked into the turf beside a rock or a tussock
animals.preferredHabitat: Open alpine turf and fellfield, especially along the edges of melting snow
animals.fact: Wind sweeps insects up off the lowlands and dumps them on the snowfields, chilled and helpless. The pipit walks the edge of the melting snow eating a meal the weather delivered uphill.
animals.role: A slim brown ground-walker that bobs its tail non-stop as it hunts across open turf. It nests in a scrape tucked beside a rock and feeds heavily on that stranded insect fallout, one of the strangest free lunches in the mountains. Foxes and ermines take it and its ground nests.

requirements.hint: Open turf to walk and nest in, and a lingering snowbank with a dark line of debris along its edge. That stripe is the dinner table.

sources.name: Birds of the World — American Pipit food habits

animals.name: Boreal Toad
animals.diet: beetles, ants, flies, springtails and other invertebrates; tadpoles graze algae
animals.shelter: Rodent burrows, rock chambers and damp cover above the breeding pools
animals.preferredHabitat: Subalpine and alpine wet meadows with shallow, sun-warmed, fish-free breeding pools
animals.fact: It spends September to May underground, then comes out and breeds in pools that were solid ice a few weeks earlier.
animals.role: The only toad living this high. Adults eat insects by the thousand and the tadpoles graze algae in shallow, sun-warmed pools, and almost nothing eats them because their skin tastes foul. What actually threatens this toad is a skin fungus and trout stocked into lakes that never had fish.

requirements.hint: Shallow warm pools to breed in and a burrow to spend the other eight months of the year in. Keep the pools fishless, because stocked trout are the single biggest reason high-country amphibians disappear.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Anaxyrus boreas
NPS Rocky Mountain NP — Where do boreal toads spend the winter?
Colorado Parks and Wildlife — Boreal Toad

animals.name: White-throated Swift
animals.diet: flying insects only — moths, beetles, flies and drifting swarms of ants, all taken in mid-air
animals.shelter: A cup of feathers glued with its own spit into a narrow crack in a cliff face
animals.preferredHabitat: Sheer cliffs and broken crags with a lot of open air in front of them to hunt in
animals.fact: It does everything in the air. It eats in the air, drinks in the air, and pairs mate in mid-air — locking together and tumbling hundreds of feet down the cliff face before they let go.
animals.role: A blade-shaped bird that lives in the sky above the mountain, hoovering up moths, beetles and whatever else the wind lifts, at speeds that make it one of the fastest birds alive in level flight. Its feet only cling, never perch, so it has to fold itself into a crack in a cliff at night, and it sticks the nest in place with its own saliva. Because it eats only what is flying, a swift working the ridge is proof the insect life below has come back. Almost nothing is quick enough to catch one.

requirements.hint: A narrow crack in a cliff to sleep in and a lot of open air in front of it. It never lands to feed and it drinks on the wing, so any pool it can skim will do.

animals.name: Mountain Chickadee
animals.diet: insects, spiders and bark-beetle larvae in summer; cached conifer seeds in fall and winter
animals.shelter: Existing cavities in dead conifers — old woodpecker holes, or soft rotten wood it can enlarge
animals.preferredHabitat: Treeline conifer forest of fir and whitebark pine with standing dead trees
animals.fact: It hides thousands of seeds one at a time and remembers where they are. The part of its brain that does the remembering actually grows bigger in autumn.
animals.role: The small busy bird that seems to be everywhere in the last trees, hanging upside down off twigs after insects and beetle grubs and switching to hidden seeds in winter. It can only nest where the wood has already gone soft, so dead trees are not mess, they are the nursery. Weasels, foxes and martens take it.

requirements.hint: Dead trees are the point. An old woodpecker hole is both shelter and a starting place — this one takes a ready-made cavity and works it wider. The whitebark pines come from its forgotten seeds.

sources.name: All About Birds — Mountain Chickadee life history

animals.name: Lynx
animals.diet: snowshoe hares above all — sometimes almost nothing else — plus white-tailed ptarmigan, ground squirrels and young marmots
animals.shelter: A hollow under boulders, roots or deadfall, often a burrow something else started and it widened
animals.preferredHabitat: High snowy country with thickets of dwarf conifer where hares can hide and lynx can wait for them
animals.fact: A lynx weighs about as much as a border collie, but its paws are as wide as a mountain lion's. They spread as it steps, so it walks on top of snow a fox would sink straight through.
animals.role: The mountain's hare specialist, and almost nothing else will do. When hares are everywhere, lynx are everywhere; when the hares crash a few years later, the lynx crash right behind them, and the whole thing swings back and forth on roughly a ten-year beat. It hunts by sitting perfectly still in the thickets and letting the hare come to it, so low tangled cover matters more to it than open ground. It rarely digs, moving instead into a hollow under rock that somebody else opened up. Eagles take its kittens.

requirements.hint: No hares, nothing doing — it really is that simple. Get the dwarf-pine thickets back so hares have somewhere to hide, and it will move into a hollow under the rocks that something else dug.

animals.name: Pine Marten
animals.diet: voles, red squirrels, pikas, hares, birds, eggs, insects and berries
animals.shelter: Dens in hollow logs, tree cavities and rock crevices, usually under deep snow
animals.preferredHabitat: Structurally complex treeline forest with big trees, dead wood and rock
animals.fact: In winter a marten hunts inside the snowpack, in the hollow spaces between the drifts and the ground, where nothing else its size can follow it.
animals.role: A cat-sized weasel equally at home in the treetops and the snow tunnels, hunting voles, pikas, young hares and birds, with berries in late summer. Structure is what it needs above everything else, so a cleared slope empties of martens even while the prey is still there. Eagles catch it.

requirements.hint: You cannot build this one's habitat out of rocks and flowers. It needs a stand of real trees, dead wood on the ground, and hares already living there.

sources.name: Alaska Department of Fish and Game — American marten

animals.name: Ermine
animals.diet: small rodents, especially voles; also young pikas, birds, eggs and insects
animals.shelter: Dens taken over from its prey — rodent burrows and rock crevices, relined with the previous owner's fur
animals.preferredHabitat: Talus and heath edges beside turf with dense rodent prey, used all year round
animals.fact: An ermine turns pure white in winter except for the black tip of its tail, and it is narrow enough to chase a vole down the vole's own tunnel.
animals.role: A weasel shaped like a furry pencil, living mostly on voles and mice and taking young pikas, nestlings and eggs besides. It builds nothing. It moves into the burrow of whatever it has just eaten and lines the nest with the previous owner's fur. It is here in every season, not only in the snow. Foxes, martens and eagles kill it in turn.

requirements.hint: It moves into a burrow it has just emptied, so bring the small rodents back first.

sources.name: Idaho Fish and Game species catalog — ermine

animals.name: Golden Eagle
animals.diet: marmots, hares, ground squirrels, white-tailed ptarmigan and other birds, plus carrion
animals.shelter: Huge stick eyries built on sheer cliff ledges and reused for decades
animals.preferredHabitat: Open, high country with big cliffs to nest on and plenty of medium-sized prey
animals.fact: A hunting golden eagle drops out of the sky at over 240 kilometres an hour, and its eyesight is sharp enough to pick a yellow-bellied marmot out of a boulder field from a kilometre up.
animals.role: The hunter that owns the air up here, taking marmots, hares and white-tailed ptarmigan in long stooping dives and killing smaller predators outright when it gets the chance. It takes newborn lambs, kids and fox cubs, but not adult sheep or goats. Its huge stick eyrie on a cliff ledge gets added to and reused for decades. Adults have nothing above them.

requirements.hint: This one comes last, when the mountain is properly alive again. It needs a real cliff for the eyrie and open ground below with plenty moving on it.

sources.name: All About Birds — Golden Eagle life history
Birds of the World — Golden Eagle food habits

animals.name: Purple Sea Urchin
animals.diet: living kelp and surfgrass, drift kelp, and encrusting coralline algae
animals.shelter: Pits it grinds into the rock itself with its teeth and spines
animals.preferredHabitat: Wave-exposed low intertidal and shallow subtidal rock near kelp
animals.fact: A purple urchin chews a pit into solid rock with five teeth and then sits in it for years. On some reefs the urchins wear away more stone than the waves do.
animals.role: The grazer at the middle of this coast's most famous story. Fed on scraps of drift kelp and kept in check by otters, urchins are just one more part of a healthy forest. Take the predators away and they march up the rock, mow the kelp to bare stone, and leave an urchin barren behind them.

requirements.hint: Kelp first — it has to have something to eat. Then think hard about what is going to eat it.

animals.name: Anchovy
animals.diet: plankton — copepods, diatoms and larvae — strained from the water or picked one at a time
animals.shelter: The school itself; open nearshore water, with kelp and surfgrass edges as nursery cover
animals.preferredHabitat: Cool, plankton-rich nearshore water over the shelf
animals.fact: An anchovy eats two ways: it snaps at big prey one bite at a time, or just opens its mouth and swims, straining the sea like a living net.
animals.role: Anchovies travel in silver schools so thick they turn the water dark from below. Almost everything that hunts here takes them at some point — pelicans, seals, dolphins, gulls — so when the anchovies fail, the whole coast goes hungry at once.

requirements.hint: Cold water rising from the deep grows the plankton they eat, and quiet shallows give the schools somewhere to spawn.

animals.name: Beach Hopper
animals.diet: decaying kelp and other stranded seaweed in the wrack line
animals.shelter: Burrows dug in damp sand high on the beach, and the damp underside of drift kelp and driftwood
animals.preferredHabitat: Gently sloping sandy beach with an undisturbed wrack line
animals.fact: Beach hoppers spend all day sealed inside a burrow in dry sand, then pour out after dark to shred the seaweed the tide left behind. Step near one and it fires itself into the air like a flicked pebble.
animals.role: The engine room of the beach. Hoppers chew stranded kelp down into crumbs and nutrients, and in doing so they turn dead seaweed into bird food — which is the entire reason plovers, sanderlings and gulls patrol the tide line. Rake the wrack away and this link vanishes overnight.

requirements.hint: Leave the seaweed where the tide drops it. That is the whole meal.

sources.name: California Conservation Genomics Project — Megalorchestia californiana

animals.name: Hermit Crab
animals.diet: algae, detritus, and scavenged carrion
animals.shelter: Borrowed empty snail shells
animals.preferredHabitat: Tidepools and low rock benches with a supply of empty snail shells
animals.fact: Hermit crabs queue up by size and swap houses in a chain: the biggest one moves into the new shell, the next takes the house it left, and so on all the way down the line until the smallest crab gets an upgrade.
animals.role: A tidepool tidier that grazes algae and cleans up dead things — and one of the shore's great recyclers, since every shell it wears is the leftover of a snail. What limits hermit crabs is almost never food. It is houses.

requirements.hint: A pool is not enough. Leave a supply of empty snail shells, or there is nothing to move into.

animals.name: Bat Star
animals.diet: algae, detritus, and dead plants and animals
animals.shelter: Rocky rubble bottoms, surfgrass beds and kelp holdfasts
animals.preferredHabitat: Shallow rocky and rubble bottom with surfgrass or kelp
animals.fact: A bat star eats by pushing its stomach out through its mouth and spreading it over its meal, digesting food outside its own body. It also refuses to stick to five arms — four to nine is perfectly normal.
animals.role: The cleanup crew of the shallows. It slides over the seafloor digesting algae, scraps and dead animals exactly where they lie, doing the same job a mushroom or an earthworm does on land — just wetter, and with more arms.

requirements.hint: Broken rock and rubble with surfgrass streaming over it. This is a rocky-bottom animal, not an eelgrass one.

animals.name: Mussel
animals.diet: plankton filtered from seawater
animals.shelter: Dense beds anchored to wave-washed rock by byssal threads
animals.preferredHabitat: Exposed rocky shore with clean, constantly moving water
animals.fact: A mussel glues itself to the rock with threads it spins out of its own foot — and if it does not like where it landed, it cuts them, crawls a little way, and glues itself down again.
animals.role: A shellfish that builds its own reef. The beds pile up thick enough that hundreds of smaller animals live in the gaps between shells, and half this shore's hunters — sea stars, oystercatchers, turnstones, otters — are really just here for the mussels.

requirements.hint: A filter feeder needs water that keeps moving. Give it surge-washed rock rather than a still pool, and barnacle crust for the young to settle on.

animals.name: Gray Whale
animals.diet: bottom-living amphipods and swarming mysid shrimp, sifted through baleen
animals.shelter: Open ocean; passes close inshore along a healthy coast
animals.preferredHabitat: Nearshore water with soft-bottom freshwater shrimp beds and mysid swarms at the kelp edge
animals.fact: Gray whales roll onto one side and vacuum the seafloor, straining out shrimp-like amphipods and leaving long muddy plumes trailing behind them — and they do it at the end of a swim of up to 14,000 miles.
animals.role: A baleen whale that feeds off the bottom rather than skimming the surface, so a whale that lingers offshore is really a report on the seabed and the kelp edge below it. Adults are far too big to be hunted here; the calves travelling with them in spring are not, and orcas know it.

requirements.hint: Give this one deep water and a seabed thick with tiny shrimp-like amphipods. Tidepools and dune plantings will never bring it in.

sources.name: Hildebrand et al. 2024, Sci Rep — urchin/kelp cascade and gray whale foraging

animals.name: Brant Goose
animals.diet: eelgrass, plus sea lettuce and other green algae
animals.shelter: Open shoreline, sandbars and shallow bays
animals.preferredHabitat: Shallow coastal bays with eelgrass beds
animals.fact: Brant fly thousands of miles to eat basically one thing: eelgrass. Lose the eelgrass in a bay and the geese are gone within a season or two, no matter how nice the rest of it looks.
animals.role: A small sea goose that grazes eelgrass and green algae in shallow bays and almost nothing else. Because it is so fussy, a bay full of brant is a bay with healthy seagrass — they are a living gauge of the meadow below them.

requirements.hint: Eelgrass to graze, and a quiet sandbar to stand on while the tide is too high to feed.

animals.name: Shore Crab
animals.diet: mostly algae and drift kelp, plus detritus, worms, snails and carrion
animals.shelter: Crevices in splash-zone rock
animals.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal and splash zone, often out of the water altogether
animals.fact: The shore crab spends more than half its life out of the sea, breathing air on dry rock, and only nips back to a pool now and then to wet its gills.
animals.role: The busiest scavenger on the highest rocks, scraping surfaces clean of algae and hauling away anything that dies. It is also breakfast for gulls, oystercatchers and turnstones, and one of the very first animals to reappear on a shore that is coming back to life.

requirements.hint: Barely any water. High rock, deep cracks to wedge into, and one pool nearby to duck into when it needs a drink.

animals.name: Gull
animals.diet: fish, crabs, mussels, sea stars and carrion
animals.shelter: Ground scrapes on offshore rocks and islands, tucked beside driftwood, rock or low coastal scrub
animals.preferredHabitat: Any shoreline with food to scavenge or catch
animals.fact: A gull that finds a mussel it cannot open carries it high into the air and drops it onto rock — and it remembers which rock cracks shells best, coming back to the same one all season.
animals.role: A bold, clever generalist that scavenges carrion and hunts crabs, shellfish, anchovies and even sea stars, tying dozens of small animals to the top of the food web. Nothing on this shore hunts a grown gull, which is exactly why it can afford to be so cheeky.

requirements.hint: Open beach to patrol, low scrub to nest beside, and one hard flat rock to bomb shellfish onto.

animals.name: Sanderling
animals.diet: beach hoppers, mole crabs, amphipods, worms and small molluscs
animals.shelter: Open beach above the surf line
animals.preferredHabitat: The wet swash zone of an open sandy beach
animals.fact: Sanderlings spend the whole day sprinting at the sea and running away from it, chasing each wave out to grab whatever it uncovered and fleeing the next one before it buries them.
animals.role: A specialist of the sliding strip of water at the sea's edge, feeding on the small crustaceans the surf keeps turning over. Its flocks live or die on how much life the wrack line produces, so a beach that is groomed clean is a beach without sanderlings.

requirements.hint: The wet strip where the waves run out, with open sand behind it. Do not plant anything here — this bird feeds where the water slides.

animals.name: Snowy Plover
animals.diet: beach invertebrates: beach hoppers, kelp flies and their larvae, small crustaceans and molluscs
animals.shelter: A shallow scrape on open sand, sometimes lined with shell fragments; chicks shelter beside driftwood and wrack
animals.preferredHabitat: Wide, flat, sparsely vegetated open sand above the tide line
animals.fact: A snowy plover's entire nest is a dent in bare sand lined with a few shell chips. The chicks run within hours of hatching, and freeze flat as pebbles the moment a shadow crosses them.
animals.role: A threatened beach nester that feeds on tiny invertebrates along the sand and the wrack. It will not nest where it cannot see a predator coming, which makes it one of the very few animals here that thick planting drives away rather than attracts — the kindest thing you can build it is emptiness nobody walks through.

requirements.hint: No water, no planting. Bare open sand, a roped-off patch where nobody treads, and driftwood for the chicks to hide beside.

animals.name: Black Turnstone
animals.diet: barnacles, limpets, small mussels, hermit crabs and other rocky-shore invertebrates
animals.shelter: Rocky shoreline; tight flocks on raised rock at high tide
animals.preferredHabitat: Rocky intertidal shores with barnacle and limpet crusts
animals.fact: A turnstone does exactly what its name promises — flips over stones, shells and clumps of seaweed to snatch whatever is hiding underneath — and hammers barnacles open with a stubby bill shaped like a chisel.
animals.role: A rocky-shore forager that pries barnacles and limpets loose and turns over wrack for hidden prey. It also needs somewhere safe to sit out high tide, when every feeding rock it owns is underwater. Take away the roosts and the shore loses its turnstones even with the food untouched.

requirements.hint: Barnacle-crusted rock to hammer at when the tide is out, and a high dry rock to stand on when it is not.

animals.name: Crow
animals.diet: crabs, shellfish, eggs, insects, fruit and whatever the tide leaves behind
animals.shelter: A bulky stick nest high in a shore pine, reused and repaired year after year
animals.preferredHabitat: The strip where the beach meets the trees, with a clear view of the tideline
animals.fact: Crows work out that a shell will break if you drop it on rock, and they pick their spot — one that has learned the trick will carry a clam up, drop it, and adjust its height until the shell cracks. They also remember faces for years.
animals.role: The sharpest bird on the shore. It patrols the tideline for anything stranded, cracks open what it can't bite through, and follows the gulls and the otters to see what they turn up.

requirements.hint: A tall tree back from the beach to nest in, and a wrack line worth patrolling. It will find everything else on its own.

animals.name: Sea Star
animals.diet: mussels above all, plus barnacles, limpets, chitons, snails and small urchins
animals.shelter: Damp surge channels and rock crevices at the lower edge of the mussel bed
animals.preferredHabitat: Wave-washed rocky intertidal with mussel beds above and surge below
animals.fact: This is the animal the word 'keystone' was invented for. Take the sea stars off a shore and within a couple of years the mussels spread down over everything else — which is precisely what happened when a wasting disease melted these stars by the million along thousands of miles of coast.
animals.role: The rocky shore's most famous predator. Working upward from the low zone and eating mussels as it goes, it decides where the mussel bed stops, and that leaves bare space on the rock for barnacles, algae, anemones and dozens of other species. Remove it and the mussels simply take everything.

requirements.hint: Build the mussel bed first, and build it big. It lives down in among the shells, along the bottom edge where the bed gives way to open rock.

sources.name: MARINe (UC Santa Cruz) — Pisaster and sea star wasting disease

animals.name: Anemone
animals.diet: crabs, detached mussels and small fish stung by its tentacles
animals.shelter: The walls and floors of surge-flushed pools, characteristically just below the mussel beds
animals.preferredHabitat: Clear, sunlit, surge-fed pools in the low zone
animals.fact: That glowing green comes from algae living inside the anemone's own body, making sugar out of sunlight and handing it over like rent. An anemone stuck in the shade goes pale and goes hungry.
animals.role: A sit-still hunter that waits below the mussel beds and catches whatever the surf knocks loose from above, while farming its own private algae for extra meals. Half its food arrives by accident, falling out of the rocks overhead.

requirements.hint: A sunlit pool with surge running through it, sitting below a mussel bed. Dinner falls in from upstairs.

sources.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium — Giant green anemone

animals.name: Puffin
animals.diet: small fish carried crosswise in its beak, plus shrimp and other small swimmers
animals.shelter: A burrow dug a metre back into the turf on top of a sea cliff
animals.preferredHabitat: Grassy clifftops above deep water, with soil soft enough to dig
animals.fact: A puffin can hold a dozen fish crosswise in its beak at once without dropping any — backward-pointing spines on its tongue and the roof of its mouth pin each one while it catches the next.
animals.role: A small seabird that lives almost its whole life out on the water and only comes ashore to nest, digging a burrow into the clifftop turf. Its beak only turns bright orange for the breeding season, then dulls again for winter.

requirements.hint: Soft turf on top of a cliff to dig a burrow into, and deep water below it full of small fish.

animals.name: Brown Pelican
animals.diet: small schooling fish, especially northern anchovy
animals.shelter: Nests only on undisturbed offshore islands; loafs on sandbars and rocks
animals.preferredHabitat: Anchovy-rich nearshore water within reach of an island colony
animals.fact: A brown pelican dives from sixty feet up and hits the water hard enough to stun fish — and it twists its body left just before impact so the blow does not break its neck.
animals.role: A plunge-diving anchovy hunter whose comeback after pesticide poisoning is one of the great conservation rescues. It nests only on islands offshore, never on the mainland beach, and its colonies fail outright in years when the anchovy schools do not show — so a nesting brown pelican is a statement about the fish, not the sand.

requirements.hint: An island the tide and the footpaths cannot reach, sandbars to loaf on, and it schools in the water offshore.

animals.name: Sea Otter
animals.diet: sea urchins above all, plus mussels, crabs and sea stars
animals.shelter: Rafts wrapped in living surface kelp canopy, in coves calm enough to groom in
animals.preferredHabitat: Kelp forest and rocky shore with abundant shellfish and calm rafting water
animals.fact: A sea otter has no blubber at all — just the thickest fur on Earth, about a million hairs in a patch the size of a postage stamp — so it spends hours a day combing air into its coat, and wraps itself in kelp so it does not drift away while it sleeps.
animals.role: The animal this whole coast hangs on. By eating urchins it stops them mowing the kelp down to bare rock, so the forest and everything sheltering in it survives. Remove the otter and the urchins multiply, the kelp goes, and what is left is a barren. Note what it rafts in: living canopy, not dead wrack on the beach.

requirements.hint: Living kelp forest to wrap up in, calm water to groom in, and urchins and shellfish to eat. Dead kelp on the sand is no use to it.

animals.name: Harbor Seal
animals.diet: fish, especially anchovy and flatfish, plus squid, octopus and crustaceans
animals.shelter: Undisturbed low-tide rocks and sandbars used as haul-outs for resting and pupping
animals.preferredHabitat: Calm, clean water beside a haul-out nobody walks up to
animals.fact: Harbor seals can sleep at sea, hanging upright just below the surface like bottles and bobbing up for a breath without properly waking.
animals.role: A patient, curious hunter that eats whatever fish is easiest to catch that week. Everything it does on land happens on a haul-out: resting, moulting, giving birth. Walk up to one once and the seals stop using it. Nothing on this shore hunts an adult seal — but something out in the deep water does.

requirements.hint: Deep water to fish in and quiet rocks to haul out on, with room around them. A haul-out is not a bird nesting closure — build the right thing.

animals.name: Desert Termite
