animals.diet: dead grass, fallen leaves, dry dung and the weathered outsides of dead wood
animals.shelter: Tunnels and chambers underground, plus mud sheeting built over whatever it is eating
animals.preferredHabitat: Soil beneath shrubs and grasses where dead plant litter collects
animals.fact: These termites plaster a thin mud roof over a dead stem and eat underneath it, so they can feed in full sun without ever touching the dry air.
animals.role: The animal that actually recycles this desert. There is too little water here for litter to rot the way it does in a forest, so termites eat almost all of it instead, carrying the nitrogen and carbon back underground and leaving tunnels that let rain soak in rather than run off. On swarm nights, everything with a beak or a sting comes to the feast.

requirements.hint: Bury a little dead wood and they will find it — dead wood is the desert’s pantry.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Physical and chemical alteration of soil by two subterranean termite species in a desert grassland

animals.name: Jackrabbit
animals.diet: grasses, wildflowers, cactus pads, and the twigs and bark of desert shrubs
animals.shelter: A shallow shaded scrape under a shrub; it never digs a burrow
animals.preferredHabitat: Open flats with scattered shrubs and room to run
animals.fact: Those enormous ears are radiators — a jackrabbit lies dead still in the shade and pours its body heat straight out through the blood vessels inside them.
animals.role: The biggest everyday plant-eater here, and the meal at the centre of everyone else's day. Its babies are born furred and open-eyed in a shallow scrape, because a jackrabbit owns no burrow and never will — it bets everything on ears, speed and knowing where the shade is.

requirements.hint: Grass to graze, shrubs to browse and a shaded scrape to lie in. Skip the water — it drinks from the plants.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service FEIS — Lepus californicus

animals.name: Kangaroo Rat
animals.diet: seeds, carried home in fur-lined cheek pouches and buried in underground larders
animals.shelter: Shallow burrows under shrubs and soil mounds, plugged with sand every dawn
animals.preferredHabitat: Loose soil under seed-bearing shrubs and mesquite
animals.fact: A kangaroo rat never drinks — it manufactures all the water it needs out of dry seeds — and it can leap sideways almost two metres to dodge a striking snake.
animals.role: The desert's accidental gardener. It buries seeds all over its patch and forgets enough of them that those are the plants that come up next spring. Its tunnels are the starting point for everything that cannot dig well: kit foxes widen them into dens, and half the burrows in the biome began as its work. Nearly every predator here eats it.

requirements.hint: Seed plants and soft diggable soil, especially the loose mounds heaped round a shrub's base. Build no water at all — this one may never take a drink in its life.

animals.name: Desert Tortoise
animals.diet: native grasses, spring wildflowers, and cactus pads and fruit
animals.shelter: Caliche caves, rock crevices and dens under boulders on rocky slopes
animals.preferredHabitat: Rocky slopes with native grasses and wildflowers
animals.fact: A desert tortoise can live 80 years and spends about 95 of every 100 days of it underground — and it carries a bladder of stored water it can live off for a year if the rains fail.
animals.role: A slow, long-lived grazer that also happens to be the landlord. The dens it hollows out get used for years afterwards by owls, snakes, lizards, rodents and insects that could never dig anything like them, so saving one tortoise quietly saves a dozen other animals. Grown tortoises are nearly untouchable; it is the hatchlings, soft-shelled for years, that ravens and coyotes take.

requirements.hint: A caliche den on a rocky slope, with grass and wildflowers to graze in front of it. It drinks only when rain puddles, and can wait a whole year for that.

sources.name: Desert Tortoise Council — Biology of Desert Tortoises

animals.name: Cactus Bee
animals.diet: pollen and nectar from prickly pear and cholla flowers
animals.shelter: A vertical nest shaft dug in bare, loose ground, often with a little mud chimney over the door
animals.preferredHabitat: Blooming prickly pear and cholla beside open, undisturbed soil
animals.fact: Every female digs her own nest and stocks it herself — but thousands of these single mothers dig side by side in the same patch of bare ground, so the whole ground hums.
animals.role: The bee that makes cactus fruit happen. No bee visits means no fruit set, and no fruit means no midsummer water for the squirrels, birds and rodents that live on it. She needs soft, undisturbed bare soil to dig in, which is exactly what hooves and tyres destroy first.

requirements.hint: Cactus flowers to work and a patch of loose, unpacked ground to dig in. Trampled hardpan is useless to her.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Cactus Bee nesting sites

animals.name: Desert Hummingbird
animals.diet: nectar from chuparosa, ocotillo and creosote flowers, plus small insects and spiders
animals.shelter: A thimble-sized cup of plant down and spider silk in a low shrub
animals.preferredHabitat: Washes and flats with shrubs that flower in winter and spring
animals.fact: The male dives past the female at full speed and shrieks — except the shriek comes from his tail feathers, not his throat — while flaring a violet moustache of feathers out sideways.
animals.role: A nectar-drinker that chases the bloom, arriving with the winter flowers of chuparosa and moving on as the desert dries out. It never needs to find water, and on the hardest days it switches itself almost off, dropping into a torpor so deep it feels cold to the touch.

requirements.hint: Real flowers beat a feeder every time: chuparosa blooms right through the desert winter, and ocotillo takes over in spring.

sources.name: Sonoran Joint Venture — Costa's Hummingbird species account
Cornell Lab All About Birds — Costa's Hummingbird Life History

animals.name: Quail
animals.diet: seeds, green leaves and cactus fruit — and, for the first weeks of life only, insects
animals.shelter: A ground nest tucked under a shrub; the covey roosts up inside thorny cover at night
animals.preferredHabitat: Thorny thickets along washes, within walking distance of water
animals.fact: One male stands sentry on a high branch with that comma of feathers bobbing on his forehead while the rest of the covey feeds below, and when he calls the alarm the whole group runs — quail would nearly always rather sprint than fly.
animals.role: A sociable ground bird living on seeds and greens, with the chicks fattened on insects for their first few weeks. Unlike almost everything else here it genuinely has to drink, so coveys walk the same path to the same water every summer day. Coyotes and hawks take adults; ravens and roadrunners take eggs and chicks.

requirements.hint: Thorny thickets to roost in and seeds to eat — and unlike most of this desert, water it can actually drink.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gambel's Quail Life History

animals.name: Cactus Woodpecker
animals.diet: insects, cactus fruit and mistletoe berries
animals.shelter: Cavities it chisels out of living saguaros
animals.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands with mesquite and washes nearby
animals.fact: It chisels a hole into a living cactus and then waits months, doing nothing, while the plant seals the raw walls with hard scar tissue — only then will it move in.
animals.role: The only animal here that can build a home from scratch, and half the biome lives in its leftovers: elf owls, kestrels, flycatchers and wild bees all move into old woodpecker holes. It also eats cactus fruit by the beakful and drops the seeds wherever it goes, so the cactus needs the bird just as much as the bird needs the cactus.

requirements.hint: Tall cactus to carve and split fruit to eat. A pad cactus is far too small — only a great column can hold a nest hole.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Gila Woodpecker Life History

animals.name: Phainopepla
animals.diet: mistletoe berries in winter, flying insects the rest of the year
animals.shelter: A small cup nest in a mesquite or ironwood, usually hidden in a clump of mistletoe
animals.preferredHabitat: Mesquite stands carrying mistletoe, with water nearby
animals.fact: A phainopepla can put away more than a thousand mistletoe berries in a single day, and the seeds come out the other end still sticky — so the bird glues the next generation of mistletoe onto branches as it flies.
animals.role: Mistletoe's one dependable gardener; almost nothing else will touch the berries. The plant only grows on mesquite, ironwood and acacia, so this glossy black bird with red eyes needs those trees as much as the mistletoe does. Out of berry season it snaps insects out of the air instead.

requirements.hint: Mistletoe in a mesquite is the whole story — the berries are dinner and the clump is the nest. It still comes down to drink.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Phainopepla Life History

animals.name: Antelope Squirrel
animals.diet: cactus fruit, seeds and green shoots, with the odd insect
animals.shelter: Burrows and cracks under rocks and cactus
animals.preferredHabitat: Rocky ground with cactus in fruit
animals.fact: It runs with its tail flipped flat over its back like a tiny parasol, then throws itself belly-down on cool shaded ground to dump the heat it picked up on the way.
animals.role: The one animal still out and about at midday, when everything else has gone underground to wait. It cannot make its own water, so it lives on juicy cactus fruit — which only exists if the cactus bees got to the flowers first. Coyotes, kit foxes, hawks, roadrunners and rattlesnakes all hunt it.

requirements.hint: Dry seeds alone will not keep it alive — it needs juicy fruit, and that means welcoming the bees first.

animals.name: Cactus Wren
animals.diet: insects and spiders, with some cactus fruit and seeds
animals.shelter: Football-shaped grass nests built deep inside a cholla
animals.preferredHabitat: Desert with dense cholla and scattered trees
animals.fact: A cactus wren builds several football-shaped nests and keeps the spare ones as bedrooms all year, so it goes to sleep surrounded on every side by cactus spines.
animals.role: The biggest wren you will ever meet, flipping over leaves and bark for insects and spiders and taking every drop of its water from that food. Its nest sits deep inside a cholla where the spines keep snakes and raiding birds out — take away the cholla and the wren has nowhere at all to raise chicks.

requirements.hint: Cholla is the nest. Nothing else out here is spiny enough, and it never once needs a drink.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Cactus Wren Life History

animals.name: Burrowing Owl
animals.diet: big insects — termites, grasshoppers and crickets — plus small rodents and scorpions
animals.shelter: Underground burrows dug by somebody else; it cannot dig its own
animals.preferredHabitat: Open ground with low, sparse plants and ready-made burrows
animals.fact: Corner a burrowing owl down its hole and it hisses like a rattlesnake — biologists think it is doing an impression, and whatever is digging usually decides not to.
animals.role: A long-legged little owl that hunts insects in broad daylight and rodents after dark, standing on its doorstep bobbing at anything that comes near. It is the clearest case here of an animal that cannot make its own home: every pair depends on a burrow something else dug, so where the diggers go, the owls go too.

requirements.hint: It cannot dig. Bring the tortoise back first and its old den becomes the front door — with low, open ground out front to hunt over.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Burrowing Owl Life History

animals.name: Horned Lizard
animals.diet: harvester ants above all — about nine mouthfuls in ten — plus termites and a few other insects
animals.shelter: Shuffles itself down into loose sand; shelters under low shrubs
animals.preferredHabitat: Open sandy ground between shrubs, near harvester ant mounds
animals.fact: Cornered, a horned lizard squirts a jet of its own blood out of the corners of its eyes — it can carry a metre — and it tastes so foul that a fox will spit and keep spitting for minutes.
animals.role: An ant specialist with a stomach far too big for its body, because harvester ants are such poor food that it has to eat hundreds every day just to break even. Those ants only build on open bare ground, so the tidier, greener and more trampled a desert gets, the faster this flat little lizard vanishes from it.

requirements.hint: No ants, nothing doing. Leave the gaps between the shrubs bare and open — that is exactly where harvester ants clear their mounds.

animals.name: Raven
animals.diet: carrion above all, plus eggs, nestlings, young reptiles, insects and cactus fruit
animals.shelter: Bulky stick nests on cliffs and in tall cactus and ironwoods — and, more and more, on power poles
animals.preferredHabitat: Open desert with tall nest structures and a reliable food supply
animals.fact: Ravens remember individual human faces and hold the grudge for years, and a pair will run a con together — one bird makes a nuisance of itself while the other robs the food.
animals.role: The cleanup crew, and the biggest human story in the biome. Roads, rubbish tips, farms and power poles hand ravens free food, water and nest platforms, so there are now far more of them than this desert could ever feed by itself — and all those extra ravens eat baby tortoises, whose shells stay soft for years. Cutting off the free lunch is now a real part of saving the tortoise.

requirements.hint: They follow whatever gets left lying around: a carcass, a tall perch, something to drink. That is all they ask for — which is exactly the trouble.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Common Raven Life History
USFWS — Environmental Assessment to Reduce Common Raven Predation on the Desert Tortoise

animals.name: Roadrunner
animals.diet: lizards, big insects, millipedes, scorpions, tarantulas, small birds, rodents and snakes
animals.shelter: A bulky stick nest a metre or two up inside a thorny shrub or cholla
animals.preferredHabitat: Open running ground broken up by thorny thickets
animals.fact: A roadrunner can outrun you — over 30 km an hour on two legs — and it kills a rattlesnake by grabbing it behind the head and beating it against a rock until it stops moving.
animals.role: The daytime terror of anything small and quick: lizards, tarantulas, scorpions, millipedes, other birds, and one of the very few birds anywhere that will pick a fight with a rattlesnake. It needs both halves of its home — open ground to sprint across and a thorn thicket high enough to keep its chicks out of a mountain lion's reach.

requirements.hint: Open ground to run flat out on and a thorn thicket to nest in, with lizards and big crawlers to chase between the two.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Greater Roadrunner Life History

animals.name: Rattlesnake
animals.diet: rodents and small mammals, with birds and lizards taken now and then
animals.shelter: Rock crevices and burrows; a deep frost-free fissure all winter
animals.preferredHabitat: Rocky shelter within striking distance of busy rodent trails
animals.fact: A rattlesnake adds a new rattle segment every time it sheds, but the old ones keep snapping off — so counting the rattles tells you nothing whatsoever about its age.
animals.role: An ambush hunter that lies beside a rodent trail for days, strikes, lets go, then follows the scent trail to the body. It may eat only once a month, which makes it a slow but relentless brake on the rodent population. Every winter it goes back to the same rock den it used last year, and the year before that.

requirements.hint: A deep winter den it can come back to every single year, warm rock to wait on, and rodents on the move nearby.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Western Diamondback Rattlesnake

animals.name: Scorpion
animals.diet: millipedes, termites, crickets, spiders, tarantulas and other scorpions
animals.shelter: A spiral burrow it digs itself, as much as two and a half metres deep
animals.preferredHabitat: Loose diggable soil with litter and stone cover to hunt across at night
animals.fact: Scorpions glow an eerie blue-green under ultraviolet light, and after decades of looking at it nobody can say for certain why.
animals.role: The heavyweight of the night shift. Big, hairy and unhurried, it takes millipedes, termites, spiders and even tarantulas, which are its own size. The rocks are only its day cover — what actually keeps it alive is a spiral burrow driven metres straight down, where it sits out most of the year. Owls and roadrunners are the ones that get it.

requirements.hint: Rocks are only the doormat. What it really needs is soil deep and loose enough to dig metres straight down into.

animals.name: Elf Owl
animals.diet: moths, beetles, crickets and scorpions
animals.shelter: Old woodpecker holes in cactus and desert trees; it cannot carve its own
animals.preferredHabitat: Saguaro stands and mesquite washes full of old woodpecker holes
animals.fact: The smallest owl in the world weighs about as much as a golf ball, and it nips the stinger off a scorpion before carrying the rest home to its chicks.
animals.role: A migratory night hunter of moths and scorpions that cannot make a hole to save its life. Every nest it has ever used was chiselled out by a woodpecker and then hardened by the cactus into a waterproof boot. Plant a whole forest of cactus and you still get no elf owls until the woodpecker has done its work.

requirements.hint: Cactus alone will not do. A woodpecker has to drill the hole first and let the plant seal it into a boot.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Elf Owl Life History

animals.name: Kit Fox
animals.diet: kangaroo rats and other rodents, jackrabbits, squirrels, lizards, insects and some fruit
animals.shelter: A cool underground den with several doors, usually a rodent burrow it has widened
animals.preferredHabitat: Open desert with loose soil and plenty of small prey
animals.fact: The smallest wild dog here weighs less than a house cat, and its ridiculous ears do two jobs at once: hearing a mouse move underground, and shedding body heat like radiators.
animals.role: A night fox that lives almost entirely on rodents and hardly ever drinks — it takes its water out of what it catches. It rarely digs a den from scratch; it moves into a kangaroo rat's burrow and enlarges it, then keeps several doors open so a mountain lion can never corner it in there.

requirements.hint: Rodents first — its den is a borrowed burrow made bigger. It never needs a drink you provide.

animals.name: Coyote
animals.diet: voles, rabbits and ground squirrels; deer fawns; also fruit, insects and carrion
animals.shelter: Raises pups in a den dug into a brushy bank, often an enlarged badger or fox burrow
animals.preferredHabitat: Open grassland and edges with brushy cover for a den and water within reach
animals.fact: Three coyotes can sound like a dozen. Each one slides its pitch around while it howls, so a small family throws up a wall of voices — biologists call it the 'beau geste' effect.
animals.role: The animal at the top of this meadow, and the most adaptable carnivore in here. It hunts voles and rabbits alone, fawns in pairs, and eats fruit, insects and carrion in between. Its return is what finally puts pressure on the foxes, badgers and deer that nothing else here could touch — and it will happily trail a digging badger to snap up whatever bolts out the far side.

requirements.hint: A den bank tucked into brushy cover, wide grass full of rabbits and voles, and water within reach. It only settles where there is already plenty to eat.

animals.name: Polyphemus Moth
animals.diet: as a caterpillar, tree leaves — oak, birch, hickory, maple, willow. The adult moth has no working mouth and never eats anything at all.
animals.shelter: Spins a tough silk cocoon wrapped in a leaf; the cocoon falls with the leaves in autumn and overwinters on the forest floor.
animals.preferredHabitat: Broadleaf woodland and woodland edge with oak, birch and hickory, and an undisturbed litter layer beneath them.
animals.fact: The adult moth has no mouth. It cannot eat a single thing — everything it will ever spend finding a mate and laying eggs was eaten months earlier, by the caterpillar.
animals.role: This moth stands for the caterpillar layer, the step nearly every forest bird depends on. Caterpillars turn tough, chewy tree leaves into soft protein, and it is caterpillars, not seeds, that woodland songbirds cram into their chicks. The adults that make it through feed bats at dusk. The cocoons spend all winter down in the fallen leaves, so a woodland raked bare in autumn throws next summer's moths out with the leaf bags.

requirements.hint: Broadleaf trees for the caterpillars to eat, and leaves left lying all winter for the cocoons hidden among them.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Antheraea polyphemus

animals.name: Wood Duck
animals.diet: acorns, seeds and aquatic plants; ducklings eat insects and snails for their first weeks
animals.shelter: Obligate cavity nester — old woodpecker holes and natural hollows in trees over or beside water
animals.preferredHabitat: Wooded ponds, sloughs and slow backwaters with big cavity trees standing in or near the water
animals.fact: A wood duckling leaves home the day after it hatches by jumping out of a hole up to fifty feet up, bouncing off the ground or water, and walking away unhurt.
animals.role: The wood duck is the clearest borrower in the forest: it cannot make a hole and cannot nest without one, so it turns up only after the woodpeckers do. It ferries acorns and pond-plant seeds between the woods and the water, and it feeds owls, raccoons and foxes. Wood ducks nearly vanished a century ago, and what still limits them is holes.

requirements.hint: An old woodpecker hole in a snag standing over quiet water, with oaks nearby for acorns.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Wood Duck life history

animals.name: Flying Squirrel
animals.diet: mostly underground truffle fungi; also lichens, acorns, tree seeds and some insects
animals.shelter: Old woodpecker cavities and natural hollows; huddles in groups through winter to stay warm
animals.preferredHabitat: Cool, closed-canopy hemlock and hardwood forest with old cavity trees and a deep fungal layer in the soil
animals.fact: Flying squirrels do not fly, they glide — and under ultraviolet light their fur glows bubblegum pink, something nobody noticed until a researcher pointed a UV torch into the trees a few years ago.
animals.role: This squirrel lives mostly on mushrooms, and mostly on underground ones it has to smell through the soil and dig up. The spores ride through it and get planted at the next set of tree roots, so squirrel, fungus and tree are one loop that keeps all three going. It cannot cut a hole either, so it sleeps in old woodpecker cavities, huddled in a heap with others for warmth — and it is the favourite meal of owls and fishers, which is how energy from the underground fungi ends up at the very top of the food web.

requirements.hint: Truffles in the soil to dig up and an old woodpecker hole to sleep in. It makes neither for itself.

sources.name: USDA Forest Service — Northern flying squirrel ecology and diet

animals.name: Pileated Woodpecker
animals.diet: carpenter ants and wood-boring beetle larvae above all; also berries and nuts
animals.shelter: Excavates a new rectangular nest cavity each year in a large dead snag, and leaves last year's behind
animals.preferredHabitat: Mature forest with large-diameter standing snags and plenty of big fallen logs on the ground
animals.fact: A pileated woodpecker chisels rectangular holes so deep into rotten trunks that a small tree can snap in half where it has been working.
animals.role: This is the forest's landlord. It carves a fresh nest hole every spring and never reuses the old one, and the leftovers become homes for wood ducks, flying squirrels, fishers, bats and owls — none of which can make a hole themselves. It needs two things a tidied forest lacks: standing snags fat enough to hold a cavity, and fallen logs rotted soft enough to fill with carpenter ants. Bring those back and a dozen other species follow it in.

requirements.hint: Big snags — plural, and thick — plus logs on the ground rotted hollow enough to tear straight into.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Pileated Woodpecker life history

animals.name: Skunk
animals.diet: beetle grubs and insects dug out of the soil, plus eggs, berries and mice
animals.shelter: A borrowed burrow or a hollow under a log, plugged with leaves in the coldest weeks
animals.preferredHabitat: Forest edges and clearings with soft diggable ground and plenty of cover
animals.fact: A skunk would much rather not spray you. First it stamps its front feet, then it hisses, then it does a handstand — and only if you ignore all three does it turn around and fire, accurately, from about three metres.
animals.role: The forest's night gardener. It spends the dark hours digging little cone-shaped holes across the floor hunting beetle grubs, turning over the soil as it goes, and almost nothing dares hunt it — except the great horned owl, which has no sense of smell worth mentioning.

requirements.hint: Soft, diggable earth full of grubs, and a hollow log to sleep the day away in. It wants somewhere to dig more than somewhere to hide.

animals.name: Fisher
animals.diet: small and medium mammals — porcupines, squirrels, hares — plus birds, carrion and fruit
animals.shelter: Dens in hollow logs and ground burrows; kits are raised in a cavity high inside a living tree
animals.preferredHabitat: Unbroken conifer and mixed forest with a closed canopy and large hollow trees
animals.fact: The fisher is one of the only animals that eats porcupines. It circles round to the face — the one place with no quills — and keeps biting until it can flip the porcupine over and reach the belly.
animals.role: The fisher treats the treetops like the ground, chasing squirrels through branches and catching flying squirrels most predators never even see, and it is the main check on porcupine numbers. Because it needs canopy that connects tree to tree and big trees hollow enough to raise kits inside, finding a fisher tells you the forest is old and joined up rather than cut into patches.

requirements.hint: Closed canopy overhead, a big living tree hollow enough to raise kits high off the ground, and squirrels and porcupines below to hunt.

animals.name: American Goldfinch
animals.diet: almost entirely seeds — thistle, sunflower, aster and grass seed
animals.shelter: A tight cup nest lashed a few feet up in a shrub, bound with spider silk and lined with thistle down
animals.preferredHabitat: Weedy fields and open ground with native thistle, sunflower and asters left standing
animals.fact: Goldfinches are such strict vegetarians that a cowbird chick sneaked into a goldfinch nest starves — it cannot survive on an all-seed diet.
animals.role: A seed specialist that waits until midsummer to nest, when thistle down is finally ready to line the cup. It feeds its chicks on seed rather than insects, which almost no other songbird does, and it scatters thistle and sunflower seed across the meadow as it feeds. Being small and everywhere makes it a favourite of bird-catching hawks.

requirements.hint: Let the sunflowers and native thistles stand and go to seed. The down is what the late nest is lined with, so don't cut them back in autumn.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — American Goldfinch
Xerces Society — Standing Up for Native Thistles

animals.name: Praying Mantis
animals.diet: live insects seized by ambush — grasshoppers, bees, butterflies and anything else that walks past
animals.shelter: Perches motionless on plants; glues a foam egg case to a stiff standing stem for the winter
animals.preferredHabitat: Meadows and flowery edges with standing vegetation to ambush from
animals.fact: A mantis has one ear, in the middle of its chest, and it is tuned to bat calls. When it hears a bat hunting it folds its wings and power-dives out of the sky.
animals.role: A sit-still ambush hunter that snaps out its spined forelegs faster than you can blink and swivels its head almost right around to watch you. It is not a pest-control specialist — it takes whatever comes past, which means grasshoppers, but also bumble bees, leafcutter bees and monarch caterpillars. Bluebirds, meadowlarks, garter snakes and bats take it in turn.

requirements.hint: Leave stiff dead stems standing through the winter. That's where the foam egg case is glued, and cutting them back in autumn cuts next summer's brood.

sources.name: NC State Extension — Challenging the conventional wisdom about praying mantids

animals.name: Bluebird
animals.diet: ground insects — caterpillars, beetles, grasshoppers — plus berries in winter
animals.shelter: Grass-lined nest inside a tree cavity, an old woodpecker hole or a nest box
animals.preferredHabitat: Grassy openings with scattered trees and low perches to drop from
animals.fact: A bluebird can spot a caterpillar on the ground from the top of a fencepost twenty metres away, drop on it, and be back on the post before you've noticed it left.
animals.role: Bluebirds hunt by perching, staring at short grass, and dropping. They cannot cut their own nest hole, so they take over holes something else made — and in a meadow with no woodpecker, that means a nest box. Volunteers putting up box trails are a large part of why this bird came back at all.

requirements.hint: It can't make its own hole. Put a box up facing open grass, keep the grass short enough to hunt over, and add berries for the winter.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — Eastern Bluebird

animals.name: American Badger
animals.diet: ground squirrels, gophers, voles and mice dug straight out of their tunnels; also insects and bumble bee nests
animals.shelter: Digs its own large burrows; one of the fastest excavators alive
animals.preferredHabitat: Open grassland with deep, stone-free, diggable soil and a rodent colony to work
animals.fact: A badger can dig itself completely out of sight in under a minute — and it sometimes hunts alongside a mountain lion, the badger going in from below while the mountain lion grabs whatever bolts out of the top.
animals.role: A carnivore that hunts by excavation, going down a squirrel or gopher tunnel after its owner. That only works in deep stone-free soil, and only where there is a rodent colony worth the digging. The big holes it leaves behind get reused by foxes, coyotes and burrowing insects for years afterwards. Adults are safe from almost everything; cubs are not.

requirements.hint: Deep stone-free soil it can tear through, wide grass on top, and a ground squirrel colony to hunt. Rock piles are the opposite of what it wants.

animals.name: Freshwater Shrimp
animals.diet: dead leaves and stems, the fungi and bacteria growing on them, and algal film scraped off plants.
animals.shelter: Among submerged litter, plant stems and the loose top layer of sediment.
animals.preferredHabitat: Shallow, well-oxygenated water with a deep drift of decaying plant litter.
animals.fact: Freshwater shrimp swim on their sides, and males carry females around piggyback for days before they mate. Lift a handful of soggy leaves out of a pond and dozens of them will be flicking about in it.
animals.role: The marsh's shredder. One shrimp chews a single dead cattail leaf into thousands of crumbs — and it is really after the fungus furring the leaf, not the leaf itself. That is how a heap of dead plants becomes food for minnows, salamander larvae and dragonfly nymphs.

requirements.hint: A drift of rotting leaves in still water is all they need.

sources.name: Biological Invasions — Potential impact of invasive amphipods on leaf litter recycling in aquatic ecosystems

animals.name: Crayfish
animals.diet: decaying plants and carcasses, live aquatic plants, snails, insect larvae and freshwater shrimp.
animals.shelter: Burrows dug into saturated banks, and gaps beneath sunken logs and stones.
animals.preferredHabitat: Slow, weedy water with woody cover and a bank soft enough to dig into.
animals.fact: Lose a claw in a fight and a crayfish just grows a new one, a little bigger at every moult, until it matches the old one. Startle it and it flips its tail and rockets backwards faster than you can grab.
animals.role: The marsh's recycler, and very nearly everybody's dinner. Crayfish shred dead plants and tidy up carcasses, turning buried gunk back into living meat — which the otter, the mink, the kingfisher, the merganser, the crane, the snapping turtle and the heron then come and take.

requirements.hint: A soft bank to tunnel into, sunken wood to hide under, and plenty of rotting plants to eat.

sources.name: Reviews in Fisheries Science — Redefining the role of crayfish in aquatic ecosystems
Oecologia — Effects of crayfish on leaf processing and invertebrate colonisation of leaves

animals.name: Freshwater Mussel
animals.diet: algae, bacteria and fine dead particles strained out of the water.
animals.shelter: Burrowed upright in stable fine sediment with only its two siphons showing.
animals.preferredHabitat: Slow, settled water over firm silt and fine sand.
animals.fact: A baby mussel has to hitchhike. It clamps onto the gills of a passing fish and rides there for weeks before dropping off to start life on the bottom — and some mother mussels wave a flap of flesh shaped like a little fish to lure a host in close.
animals.role: The marsh's water filter, and one of the longest-lived animals in it. One mussel can strain the same patch of water for thirty years, dropping what it catches to the bottom for shrimp and crayfish. No fish means no baby mussels, so the mussels only come back after the minnows do.

requirements.hint: A settled bed that stays put for years — and fish, because young they ride to their new home clamped to fish gills.

sources.name: NC Wildlife — General Life History for Mussels

animals.name: Leopard Frog
animals.diet: insects, spiders and worms taken in wet meadows and along the water's edge
animals.shelter: Shallow water in spring; damp grassy meadow through the summer
animals.preferredHabitat: Lily-fringed shallows with wet meadow beside them
animals.fact: A startled leopard frog leaps in zig-zags away from the water instead of towards it — and the second it lands in long grass those big dark spots break its outline up and it vanishes.
animals.role: The frog that leaves the pond. It spends the whole summer hunting insects out in damp meadow and only hops back to the water in autumn, which is why a marsh mown right to the waterline loses its leopard frogs first.

requirements.hint: A lily pool to breed in and a wide band of damp meadow beside it to spend the whole summer hunting in.

sources.name: National Park Service — Northern Leopard Frog

animals.name: Marsh Wren
animals.diet: insects and spiders picked from marsh stems
animals.shelter: Woven dome nests lashed among cattails and bulrushes
animals.preferredHabitat: Cattail and bulrush stands over water
animals.fact: A male marsh wren builds up to a dozen empty practice nests for one female to come and inspect — and while he is at it he will sneak into a neighbour's nest and punch holes in the eggs.
animals.role: A thumb-sized bird with an enormous attitude. It runs up and down reed stems picking off spiders and insects, stitches hanging ball nests between the stiff stalks, and robs the eggs of anything that nests too close.

requirements.hint: Bulrush and cattail standing in water — stiff stems it can weave a hanging ball nest between.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Marsh Wren life history

animals.name: Snapping Turtle
animals.diet: carrion, fish, crayfish, aquatic plants and almost anything else it can catch
animals.shelter: Muddy pond bottoms; females travel overland to sandy banks to nest
animals.preferredHabitat: Deep still water with a soft mud bottom and a sandy rise to nest on
animals.fact: A snapping turtle is too big to pull into its own shell, so it does not bother trying. Underwater it is calm and shy and will swim away from you — the famous snap only comes out when it is stranded on dry land with nowhere left to hide.
animals.role: The marsh's bulldozer and its clean-up crew, walking the bottom eating carrion, plants, fish and the occasional duckling. Grown adults are almost untouchable; it is the eggs everything digs up, which is why one good nest bank matters more than any single old turtle.

requirements.hint: Deep still water with a soft bottom, plus a warm sandy rise above the waterline for the females to dig their nests in.

animals.name: Kingfisher
animals.diet: small fish and crayfish
animals.shelter: Tunnel burrows dug a metre or more into bare earthen banks
animals.preferredHabitat: Clear water with a bare vertical bank beside it and perches overhead
animals.fact: A kingfisher shuts its eyes just before it hits the water, so the last part of the dive is flown blind from memory. Then it whacks the fish against a branch and swallows it head-first so the fins fold the right way.
animals.role: The rattling plunge-diver of the marsh, and one of the rare birds where the female is the flashier of the pair. It digs its own nest tunnel a metre back into a bare earth bank, so a marsh stuffed with fish but with no raw bank still gets no kingfishers.

requirements.hint: Clear open water to dive into and a bare vertical earth bank to tunnel into. A nest box is no use to a bird that digs its own.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Belted Kingfisher life history

animals.name: Merganser
animals.diet: small fish, crayfish, dragonfly nymphs and other aquatic insects
animals.shelter: Tree cavities in standing dead timber over or beside water
animals.preferredHabitat: Quiet ponds with drowned standing trees
animals.fact: Merganser ducklings jump out of a tree hole up to fifteen metres above the ground the day after they hatch, bounce off the leaf litter unhurt, and are diving for their own food within a day of landing.
animals.role: A tiny diving duck with a fold-out white fan on its head, a saw-edged bill for gripping slippery fish, and a clear third eyelid it wears like swimming goggles. It nests in holes in drowned trees, which makes a beaver pond exactly its sort of place.

requirements.hint: A wooded pond with dead trees still standing in it. The hen wants a hole in a drowned alder — a nest box is only a stand-in.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Hooded Merganser life history

animals.name: Pillbug
animals.diet: dead leaves, rotting wood, grass thatch and fungal threads; also droppings and old bones for minerals
animals.shelter: Hides by day under crumbling logs, flat stones and deep litter, where the air stays damp
animals.preferredHabitat: Shaded, damp corners of meadow with rotting wood and a thick layer of dead plant litter
animals.fact: A pillbug is not an insect at all — it's a crustacean, closer kin to a crab than to a beetle, and it still breathes through gill-like flaps that have to stay wet.
animals.role: Pillbugs work the night shift under logs and thatch, shredding dead leaves and soft rotten wood into crumbs small enough for fungi and bacteria to finish off. That shredding is the first step in turning last year's meadow into next year's soil. Garter snakes and killdeer hunt them, so the recycling crew feeds upward as well as downward.

requirements.hint: Damp, dark and rotting is the whole recipe — a crumbling log, deep thatch, and ground that never dries right out. Roll one over and it curls into a ball.

animals.name: Garden Spider
animals.diet: flying and jumping insects caught in the web — grasshoppers, bees, flies, moths
animals.shelter: Hangs head-down at the hub of its own orb web, slung between tall standing stems
animals.preferredHabitat: Sunny meadow with tall stiff vegetation left standing and plenty of flying insects
animals.fact: This spider takes down most of its web every night and eats the old silk to build the next one — and it stitches a bold white zigzag through the middle that nobody has fully explained yet.
animals.role: The meadow's trapper. It slings a wheel of silk wider than your hand between tall stems and waits head-down at the hub for grasshoppers, bees and flies to blunder in. Spiders are the largest predator group in any grassland and the biggest single thing missing from this meadow until now — they eat enormous numbers of insects, and they are in turn the main food of half the songbirds here.

requirements.hint: Tall stiff stems left standing, spaced far enough apart to sling a big web between them, with flowers close by to bring the insects in.

sources.name: UF/IFAS Featured Creatures — yellow garden spider

animals.name: Brown Bat
animals.diet: night-flying insects, especially beetles, plus moths, flying ants and midges
animals.shelter: Roosts by day in warm dark spaces — barn lofts, attics, and under loose bark; hibernates in cold cracks
animals.preferredHabitat: Open meadow and hedgerow airspace to hunt over, with still water to drink from and a warm roost nearby
animals.fact: A big brown bat finds a moth in total darkness by shouting and listening to the echo — and it can pick out something no thicker than a pencil lead this way.
animals.role: The night shift over the meadow. Big brown bats work the air above the grass and along the hedgerows after sunset, catching beetles, moths and flying ants; one bat can put away thousands of insects in a single night. They drink on the wing, dipping their jaws into still water without stopping, and mothers gather in warm roosts to raise pups together. Great horned owls catch them at dusk.

requirements.hint: A warm crevice to raise pups in, insects in the air above the grass, and calm open water it can skim a drink from without landing.

sources.name: Bat Conservation International — Big Brown Bat

animals.name: Barn Owl
animals.diet: almost entirely small mammals under about 100 grams — voles, mice and shrews
animals.shelter: Nests and roosts in a dark high cavity: a barn loft, a hollow tree, or a large nest box. Builds nothing itself
animals.preferredHabitat: Wide open grassland to hunt over, with a dark cavity above ground to sleep and nest in
animals.fact: A barn owl can catch a mouse in complete darkness by sound alone. One ear sits higher than the other, so it hears in three dimensions — and the fringed edges of its wings mean the mouse never hears it coming.
animals.role: The meadow works a night shift, and the barn owl runs it. While the hawk and the mountain lion hunt by daylight, this one quarters the same grass in the dark on silent wings, living almost entirely on voles — a single family can take well over a thousand of them in a year. Nothing here hunts the barn owl back.

requirements.hint: A dark loft or a deep box up off the ground, wide grass to quarter over, and a meadow already full of voles. It takes its water from its prey.

sources.name: Cornell All About Birds — American Barn Owl
American Ornithological Society — 65th Supplement to the Check-list

animals.name: Mountain Lion
animals.diet: deer and wild sheep mostly, plus jackrabbits, foxes and anything else it can get close enough to
animals.shelter: No fixed home; the kittens are hidden in a dry cave or overhang in a canyon wall
animals.preferredHabitat: Broken canyon country with ledges, boulders and brush to stalk through, and somewhere reliable to drink
animals.fact: The biggest cat out here cannot roar. It purrs like a house cat, screams like something out of a nightmare, and can jump five metres straight up onto a ledge from standing.
animals.role: The top of the desert food chain and a pure ambush hunter — it does not chase things down, it gets close and then explodes. Because it kills by stalking, it needs broken ground and brush to hide in; out on the open flat it goes hungry. It drags a big kill into cover and buries it under sticks and sand to come back to for days, which quietly feeds ravens, foxes and half the beetles in the wash. Kittens spend their first weeks tucked into a cave in a canyon wall, and nothing out here hunts a grown lion.

requirements.hint: Big prey first, then rough broken ground to stalk through and a sheltered overhang for the kittens. Unlike most things out here it does come down to drink.

animals.name: Snail
animals.diet: dead leaves, soft rotting stems, and the algae film on damp stones
animals.shelter: Seals itself to the underside of a damp log or stone and waits out dry weather
animals.preferredHabitat: Shady, damp corners with leaf litter and something chalky to rasp at
animals.fact: A snail carries its own house and can shut the door behind it — when things get dry it glues itself to a stone and sleeps until it rains, sometimes for months.
animals.role: Snails are the meadow's slow recyclers. They shred fallen leaves into crumbs that fungi and soil life can finish off, and their shells give calcium back to the ground when they die.

requirements.hint: A shady damp corner where leaves are allowed to pile up and rot. It wants the mess, not the tidy bit.

animals.name: Mountain Goat
animals.diet: grasses, sedges and alpine forbs in summer; lichen, moss and shrub twigs scraped off rock in winter
animals.shelter: Beds scraped out on narrow cliff ledges and in shallow caves under overhangs
animals.preferredHabitat: The steepest broken cliff and ledge ground above the treeline, with turf to graze and a mineral seep within reach
animals.fact: A mountain goat's hooves split apart as it steps, gripping stone like the rubber on climbing shoes, and it will sleep on a ledge no wider than a doormat with a 300-metre drop underneath it.
animals.role: The white climber of the high cliffs, grazing turf and lichen and then retreating onto ground so steep that almost nothing can follow. That is the whole trick: goats live where other big grazers simply cannot go. They will walk for hours to a mineral lick and shove each other around at it. Mountain lions are the real threat, while eagles and wolverines take kids. In some ranges goats are native and in others people brought them in, so a white goat on a skyline is not always a local.

requirements.hint: Steeper is better. Give it cliff ledges to bed on, turf to graze between them, and a mineral lick, because it will travel for hours to eat salty ground. Do not expect one out on the open flats.

animals.name: Wolverine
animals.diet: marmots, hares and white-tailed ptarmigan when it can catch them, frozen carcasses when it cannot, and berries in late summer
animals.shelter: Tunnels dug metres down into deep spring drifts, usually around a fallen boulder or log, with food stored in side chambers
animals.preferredHabitat: Big, empty, high country with talus and broken rock, and snow that lasts into late spring
animals.fact: A wolverine can smell a dead animal buried under three metres of snow, dig it out, and then drive a bear off it, all in a body about the size of a small dog.
animals.role: The largest weasel in the world and the mountain's great scavenger, now the top hunter on these peaks. It roams enormous distances, kills marmots, hares and white-tailed ptarmigan when it gets the chance and lives off frozen carcasses when it does not, cracking frozen bone with jaws built for exactly that. Snow is its refrigerator: it stores food in drifts and dens deep inside them, so a female can only raise kits where the snowpack holds into late spring. That makes it the first animal to go when winters get short — and nothing up here is willing to argue with it over a carcass.

requirements.hint: It needs space and snow, not scenery. Give it drifts deep enough to last into late spring for the den and the larder, broken rock to travel through, and marmots and hares already on the mountain.

animals.name: Sea Turtle
animals.diet: seagrass above all — eelgrass and surfgrass — plus sea lettuce and other soft algae
animals.shelter: Sleeps wedged under ledges or resting on quiet sand and gravel bottom between grazing trips
animals.preferredHabitat: Warm summer water in a sheltered bay with seagrass meadows to graze
animals.fact: Adult green sea turtles are the only sea turtles that eat plants, and their jaws are serrated like bread knives for sawing through seagrass. They crop the same patch again and again, which keeps it short and tender — a turtle basically mows a lawn on the seafloor.
animals.role: A summer visitor that swims in from warmer water to eat, not to nest — no turtle lays eggs on a cool coast like this one. Grazing adults keep the seagrass cropped and growing fresh instead of going long and shaggy, and they are the only animal here besides the brant that eats a seagrass meadow for a living.

requirements.hint: This one comes for the grazing, not the sand, so do not build it a nest beach. Warm summer water, a cropped grazing lawn out in the eelgrass, and quiet bottom to sleep on between meals.

animals.name: Bottlenose Dolphin
animals.diet: schooling fish, especially anchovy, plus squid and bottom fish
animals.shelter: None built — travels and sleeps at sea in a small group, half its brain awake at a time
animals.preferredHabitat: Nearshore water along an open beach with a strong surf line and fish schools offshore
animals.fact: Every dolphin invents its own signature whistle, and the others copy that whistle back when they want to call it over. Along an open beach these dolphins hunt right inside the breakers, surfing the waves they are herding fish against.
animals.role: Fast, social hunters that work the surf line in small groups, pushing anchovy schools up against the breaking waves until the fish have nowhere left to go. They are quick and clever enough to catch almost anything that schools here — and still not the biggest thing in the water.

requirements.hint: Deep water to travel through, cold currents and kelp edges to hold the fish, and a real breaking surf line, because that is where this one does its hunting.

sources.name: Janik & King 2013, Proc R Soc B — Vocal copying of individually distinctive signature whistles

animals.name: Orca
animals.diet: marine mammals — harbor seals above all, plus dolphins, sea lions and gray whale calves
animals.shelter: None ashore; rests at the surface in deep water with its family pod
animals.preferredHabitat: Cold deep water close inshore, along the drop-off and the kelp edge within reach of seal haul-outs
animals.fact: Orcas live in families that never split up, and different families eat completely different food. The ones that hunt this coast are mammal specialists, and they go silent to do it — no clicks, no calls — because a seal can hear a talking orca coming from a long way off.
animals.role: The top of this coast, with nothing above it. A pod of mammal-hunting orcas patrols the drop-off where the seafloor falls away, listening at seal haul-outs and shadowing gray whales that pass through with calves in spring. When they come into a bay, every seal on the rocks goes still and silent.

requirements.hint: Deep water pressed right up against the shore and something big to hunt — so bring the seals back first, because the seals are what it comes for.

animals.name: Desert Millipede
animals.diet: dead leaves, stems, seed husks and other dry plant litter on the ground
animals.shelter: Buried in soil and tucked under litter and rock slabs by day; out walking on damp nights
animals.preferredHabitat: Litter drifts under shrubs with rock slabs and diggable soil nearby
animals.fact: A desert millipede spends most of the year underground, then comes pouring out by the hundreds after the first summer storm — and if you touch one it coils into a tight spiral like a cinnamon bun and oozes a bitter brown liquid that stains your fingers for days.
animals.role: The litter shredder. It chews dead leaves, stems and husks into crumbs small enough for termites and soil microbes to finish, which is how dead plants become soil again out here. It has hundreds of legs and absolutely no hurry — armour and a foul chemical mean it can afford to stroll — but scorpions and roadrunners eat it anyway.

requirements.hint: Let the leaves drift up under the shrubs and leave a slab it can crawl beneath. Damp litter is both its dinner and its hiding place — bare hot sand is neither.

sources.name: Arizona-Sonora Desert Museum — Millipedes and Centipedes

animals.name: Desert Tarantula
animals.diet: crickets, beetles, grasshoppers, termites and other spiders
animals.shelter: A silk-lined burrow in firm soil, its doorway strung with trip-lines
animals.preferredHabitat: Firm open ground between shrubs with litter and cover close by
animals.fact: A frightened desert tarantula rubs its back legs over its belly and flicks off a cloud of barbed hairs that itch like fibreglass — and if nothing comes past to eat, it can simply wait, going a whole year between meals.
animals.role: A patient ambush hunter that lives at the mouth of a silk-lined burrow, feeling for the twitch of a cricket on the trip-lines at its door. A female may keep the same hole for twenty years, which makes her one of the longest-lived animals in the biome. Roadrunners take them — and so does the giant hairy scorpion, which outweighs a desert tarantula and is not remotely afraid of one.

requirements.hint: Firm ground it can line with silk, and then quiet. A burrow it digs is one she may still be sitting in twenty years from now.

animals.name: Desert Hawk
animals.diet: jackrabbits, ground squirrels, quail, woodrats and lizards
animals.shelter: A bulky stick nest wedged in the arms of a tall cactus or a thorny tree, built and guarded by the whole family
animals.preferredHabitat: Open scrub with tall cactus and trees to nest and keep lookout from
animals.fact: These are the only birds of prey in the world that hunt in packs: a family of five or six spreads out, some crashing into a thorn bush to panic a rabbit while the others wait on the far side. And when there is nowhere decent to perch, they simply stand on each other's backs, three hawks high.
animals.role: The daytime top predator, working the same desert the mountain lion works at night. Two or three generations live together all year, share every kill, help feed each other's chicks and take turns on lookout — teamwork that lets them bring down jackrabbits far heavier than any single hawk. They need tall lookouts above open ground and a big cactus solid enough to hold a family nest.

requirements.hint: One bird is never the whole story. A family needs a tall cactus strong enough to hold the nest, high lookouts all around it, and open ground with rabbits crossing it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Harris's Hawk Life History

animals.name: Elk
animals.diet: grass and leafy plants through the growing season; twigs, buds, bark and acorns once the green is gone
animals.shelter: No den — beds down in thick conifer cover by day and moves out into open gaps to feed at dawn and dusk
animals.preferredHabitat: Big blocks of forest broken by clearings and young regrowth to graze, thick cover to rest in, and a muddy wallow within a day's walk
animals.fact: A bull elk grows a whole new set of antlers every year, laying down up to an inch of bone a day — the fastest-growing bone of any animal — and drops the lot each spring. In autumn he bugles: a squeal that carries more than a mile from an animal the size of a horse.
animals.role: The elk is this forest's big grazer, and the only animal here that eats grass in bulk. Where a squirrel nibbles and a porcupine peels bark, a herd of elk crops whole clearings, keeping gaps open and sunlit so the plants and insects of the forest edge have somewhere to live — and grazing them bare if there are too many. Elk churn wallows into muddy pools that frogs and insects then breed in, carry seeds in their coats and droppings, and their calves are one of the few big meals a bear can find in spring. Elk vanished from these woods for more than a century and are back only where people put them back.

requirements.hint: Grassy gaps and young regrowth to graze, thick cover to rest in, and a muddy wallow to roll in — a bull plasters himself in mud before he starts bugling.

animals.name: Towhee
animals.diet: insects, spiders and millipedes kicked out of the leaf litter, plus seeds, berries and bits of acorn
animals.shelter: Nests on the ground in dead leaves beneath a bramble or dense shrub, the cup sunk level with the surface
animals.preferredHabitat: Brushy tangles, forest edges and sunlit gaps where young growth is thick and the ground is deep in fallen leaves
animals.fact: That loud rustling in the dead leaves usually isn't a deer — it's a bird the size of your hand, kicking backwards with both feet at once to flip the leaves over and see what's underneath.
animals.role: The towhee works a layer nothing else in this forest bothers with: the top couple of inches of dead leaves. Its two-footed backwards kick turns litter over and over while it hunts the insects, spiders and millipedes hiding there, and the seeds and berries it swallows come back out along the brushy edges. Because the nest sits flat on the ground, the towhee feeds foxes and snakes — and it can only nest where the brush overhead is thick enough to hide a cup of grass.

requirements.hint: Thick young brush standing over a deep, unraked leaf layer. The nest goes on the ground, so the tangle above it has to be dense enough to hide it.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Eastern Towhee life history

animals.name: Water Strider
animals.diet: insects and spiders trapped in the surface film, plus mosquito larvae hanging just underneath it.
animals.shelter: Sheltered, wind-free water; overwinters tucked under bank litter and floating debris.
animals.preferredHabitat: Smooth, calm pockets of open water out of the wind, with floating stems to rest and lay eggs on.
animals.fact: Water striders do not swim — they stand on the water. Thousands of tiny hairs on each foot trap air and refuse to get wet, and the strider reads ripples the way a spider reads its web to find insects thrashing on the surface.
animals.role: The marsh's surface patrol, and one of the first animals back once the water is clean and still. Striders skate over the film eating whatever falls in and cannot climb out, and they are themselves easy pickings for minnows, frogs, dragonflies and blackbirds.

requirements.hint: This one needs calm. Find a pocket of water the wind cannot ruffle, with floating stems on it to rest and lay eggs on.

sources.name: Nature — The hydrodynamics of water strider locomotion

animals.name: Bald Eagle
animals.diet: mostly fish, plus ducks, muskrats and carrion — and anything it can bully out of another hunter's grip
animals.shelter: A huge stick nest in the crown of the tallest living tree beside open water, added to every year
animals.preferredHabitat: Wide open water full of fish, with one very tall tree to watch it all from
animals.fact: A bald eagle would honestly rather rob than fish. It shadows otters and herons and harasses them until they drop their catch, then takes it — and the nest it rebuilds every year can end up heavier than a small car.
animals.role: The top predator of the marsh and its biggest bully. It takes fish, ducks and muskrats for itself, kills herons at their nesting colonies, and spends much of the day stealing meals from otters and herons — which means it can only settle somewhere those hunters are already doing well.
eatsOther: fish stolen from otters and herons

requirements.hint: One huge old tree with a clear view over deep water, enough fish to live on — and successful otters and herons below to steal from.

sources.name: Cornell Lab All About Birds — Bald Eagle life history

animals.name: Luna Moth
animals.diet: hickory, walnut, sweetgum and birch leaves as a caterpillar; the adult eats nothing at all
animals.shelter: A papery cocoon spun inside a curled leaf that falls to the ground, where it lies buried in the litter all winter
animals.preferredHabitat: Mature deciduous woodland with deep undisturbed leaf litter under the host trees
animals.fact: An adult luna moth has no mouth. It hatches out with about a week to live, never eats once, and spends the whole of it looking for a mate.
animals.role: Luna moth caterpillars are leaf-eaters that turn tree leaves into fat, high-energy insect bodies, and everything from bats to jays cashes that in. The long twisted tails on the hindwings are an anti-bat device: they spin as the moth flies and throw a bat's echolocation off target, so the bat grabs a tail streamer instead of the body. Because the cocoon overwinters in fallen leaves, a forest that gets raked loses its luna moths even if every host tree is still standing.

requirements.hint: Plant the leafy trees, then let the leaves lie where they fall. The cocoons spend the whole winter down in that litter.

sources.name: Butterflies and Moths of North America — Actias luna

animals.name: Blue Jay
animals.diet: acorns and beechnuts, caterpillars, beetles and other insects, and eggs or nestlings when it finds them
animals.shelter: A cup of twigs and rootlets wedged in a fork high in a leafy tree, screened by foliage
animals.preferredHabitat: Oak-rich woodland and its edges, with open ground nearby for caching
animals.fact: Blue jay feathers are not actually blue — the pigment in them is brown, and the blue is a trick of light bouncing off tiny air pockets. Crush one and the colour disappears.
animals.role: A single blue jay can carry five acorns at a time and bury a few thousand in an autumn, and it chooses sound ones and pushes them into open ground — which makes jays the fastest tree planters in the forest and the reason oaks spread uphill after a fire. Jays also mimic hawk calls, sometimes to clear a feeding spot and sometimes to warn everything nearby that a real hawk has arrived, so the whole wood listens to them.

requirements.hint: Oaks and a patch of soft open ground to bury the acorns in. Some of the ones it forgets will be your next oak trees.

animals.name: Wood Frog
animals.diet: beetles, spiders, slugs, flies and other small forest-floor invertebrates
animals.shelter: Shallow leaf litter and loose duff on the forest floor — it does not burrow below the frost line
animals.preferredHabitat: Damp deciduous forest with fishless woodland pools that fill in spring and dry out by late summer
animals.fact: A wood frog freezes solid every winter. Its heart stops, two thirds of the water in its body turns to ice, and in spring it thaws out and hops away.
animals.role: Wood frogs are the first amphibian to call in spring, breeding in temporary pools that dry up before fish can ever live in them — which is exactly why the tadpoles survive. Sugar flooding the blood keeps their cells from bursting while they are frozen, so they can hibernate under a few centimetres of leaves. As adults they eat their way through the invertebrates of the leaf litter and are eaten in turn by snakes and raccoons, moving forest-floor energy up the food chain.

requirements.hint: A pool that dries up in summer is the good kind — no fish means the tadpoles live. Keep deep leaves nearby for them to freeze in.

animals.name: Goshawk
animals.diet: squirrels, jays, grouse, rabbits and woodpeckers, chased down inside the trees
animals.shelter: A broad stick nest built against the trunk on a heavy limb, halfway up a big old tree in closed canopy
animals.preferredHabitat: Mature forest with a high closed canopy and open flying room underneath it
animals.fact: A goshawk hunts by crashing straight through the branches at full speed with its wings half folded, and it will dive at anything — including people — that walks too near its nest.
animals.role: The goshawk is the forest's top daytime hunter and the reason squirrels freeze against tree trunks. Short broad wings and a long steering tail let it turn inside a wood at speed, so unlike a soaring hawk it hunts under the canopy rather than above it. It needs old forest with big limbs to nest on and clear space beneath to fly, which makes its arrival a sign that the trees have finally grown up.

requirements.hint: Grow the forest tall and leave the understory open. It needs a big limb to nest on and room to fly hard between the trunks.

animals.name: Moose
animals.diet: submerged pondweed and water lilies in summer, willow and aspen twigs in winter
animals.shelter: Beds pressed into willow thickets and shaded marsh edge; in summer it stands chest-deep in water to escape flies
animals.preferredHabitat: Marsh and pond edge with deep willow thickets and clear shallow water full of submerged plants
animals.fact: A moose can hold its breath for a minute and walk along the bottom of a pond with its whole head underwater, pulling up plants by the roots.
animals.role: Moose come to the wetland for sodium, which the submerged plants have and the forest browse does not, and a big one can pull 20 kilograms of pondweed a day out of the shallows. That heavy grazing keeps open lanes through the plant beds where ducks feed and fish shelter, and the willow they browse in winter grows back thicker and lower — which is better cover for everything small. Their trails through the marsh become channels that hold water in dry summers.

requirements.hint: Grow the underwater plant beds first and keep the water clear. It comes for what is growing under the surface, not on the bank.

sources.name: National Park Service, Isle Royale — Moose

animals.name: River Cooter
animals.diet: pondweed, algae, water lily leaves and fallen fruit; hatchlings take insects before switching to plants
animals.shelter: Sleeps wedged under submerged logs and root tangles; spends the winter buried in the mud of the pond bottom
animals.preferredHabitat: Slow, plant-filled water with logs to bask on and an open sunlit bank to lay eggs in
animals.fact: Whether a cooter's eggs hatch into males or females depends on how warm the nest is, not on the eggs themselves — a cool nest makes brothers, a warm one makes sisters.
animals.role: The cooter is the wetland's big plant-eating turtle, cropping the underwater meadows and keeping them from choking the shallows, and passing seeds out intact somewhere else. It has to bask for hours to get warm enough to digest all that plant food, which is why a good log stacked with turtles is a sign of a working marsh. Its eggs and hatchlings feed almost everything else, so it lays a lot of them.

requirements.hint: Logs in the sun to bask on and a bare warm bank to bury eggs in. One that cannot get warm cannot digest its dinner.

animals.name: Javelina
animals.diet: prickly pear pads, mesquite pods, agave hearts, roots and tubers
animals.shelter: Beds down as a herd in the shade of dense thornscrub or a rock overhang through the heat of the day
animals.preferredHabitat: Desert scrub and washes with thick thorny cover and stands of prickly pear
animals.fact: A javelina eats prickly pear whole — spines and all — and has a scent gland on its back so strong that a herd can find each other in the dark by smell alone.
animals.role: Javelinas are the desert's cactus processors: they crunch through pads that nothing else will touch, which keeps prickly pear from taking over a wash and spreads its seeds in their droppings. Rooting for tubers turns over hard-crusted soil and buries litter, giving seeds somewhere to germinate after rain. They travel in herds of six to a dozen, and the herd smell is also the alarm system, because their eyesight is terrible.

requirements.hint: Grow the prickly pear and leave a shaded thorny tangle to bed down in. A herd sleeps out the middle of the day and feeds at dusk.

animals.name: Black Swift
animals.diet: flying ants, aphids, beetles and mayflies caught on the wing, often hundreds of metres up
animals.shelter: A cup of moss glued to a wet rock seam behind or beside falling water, reached only from the air
animals.preferredHabitat: Cliffs with cold running water and wide open sky above the treeline
animals.fact: A black swift can stay in the air for six months without landing once — it eats, drinks and sleeps flying, and the chick is left alone all day while its parents hunt insects 50 km away.
animals.role: Swifts hoover up the swarming insects that get lifted onto the mountain by rising air, and they carry that food back as a compressed pellet — one delivery a day is enough for a chick because the load is so concentrated. The nest has to be permanently wet and unreachable, so the birds only appear where there is a cliff seam with water running over it. They are among the very last summer visitors to arrive and the first to leave for the Amazon.
eatsOther: aphids carried up on the wind

requirements.hint: Find the wettest, darkest crack in the cliff and keep the water running down it. This one will not nest anywhere it can walk to.

animals.name: Peregrine Falcon
animals.diet: other birds taken in mid-air — white-tailed ptarmigan, rosy-finches, swifts, pipits and small ducks
animals.shelter: A bare scrape kicked into gravel on a high cliff ledge; it builds no nest at all
animals.preferredHabitat: Sheer cliffs and rock faces overlooking open ground with plenty of birds flying below
animals.fact: A stooping peregrine hits about 380 km/h, which makes it the fastest animal alive — and it has bony cones in its nostrils that slow the air down so the dive does not burst its lungs.
animals.role: The peregrine is the mountain's aerial hunter, and it takes almost all of its food in the air, striking from above with a closed fist rather than grabbing. Because it hunts birds and nothing else, it is a direct check on the flocks of finches, pipits and white-tailed ptarmigan feeding across the slopes. It needs an undisturbed cliff ledge and clear air below it, and nothing at all to build with — just loose gravel to scrape a hollow in.

requirements.hint: A high ledge with loose gravel on it and open sky underneath. Do not build a nest — this one just kicks a dip in the grit.

animals.name: Sand Dollar
animals.diet: algae, plankton and scraps of food picked out of the sand grain by grain
animals.shelter: Half buried on edge in rippled sand, in beds of hundreds at a time
animals.preferredHabitat: Sheltered sandy bottoms just below the low tide line, where the current is gentle
animals.fact: A living sand dollar is not white and smooth — it is purple and covered in tiny moving spines it uses to walk and to pass food along to its mouth. The white disc with the flower pattern is its skeleton, after everything else has washed away.
animals.role: A whole bed of them stands half-buried on edge like coins in a slot, all leaning into the current to catch what drifts past. Where the water is rougher they lie flat instead so they do not get rolled away.

requirements.hint: Clean rippled sand just below the tide line, somewhere sheltered enough that the current is gentle.

animals.name: Octopus
animals.diet: shore crabs, clams, mussels, snails and shrimp, cracked open or drilled through
animals.shelter: A crevice or empty shell it pulls a rock across behind itself, with a heap of emptied shells outside the door
animals.preferredHabitat: Rocky subtidal seafloor and deep tidepools with plenty of crevices and cold, clean water
animals.fact: An octopus has three hearts, blue blood, and tastes everything it touches with its arms — and because the only hard part of it is its beak, one the size of a dinner plate can squeeze through a hole the size of a grape.
animals.role: The octopus is the top invertebrate hunter of the rocky shore, and the pile of emptied crab and clam shells outside its den is the easiest way to find one. It can change colour and skin texture in under a second to vanish against rock or kelp, despite being colourblind, and it will drill a neat hole through a stubborn clam and inject it to make the shell relax. Each octopus works through a huge number of crabs, which keeps the grazers and scavengers of the tidepools in check.

requirements.hint: Broken rock with gaps to hide in, and plenty of crabs. Leave the shell pile outside the den alone — that is how you know somebody is home.

sources.name: Monterey Bay Aquarium — East Pacific red octopus

animals.name: Grizzly Bear
animals.diet: roots and berries dug out of the slope, ground squirrels and marmots, winter-killed carcasses — and moths, by the hundred thousand
animals.shelter: Digs a den into a high slope in autumn and sleeps in it until the snow softens
animals.preferredHabitat: Open high country with digging ground, berry slopes and no people
animals.fact: Grizzlies climb above the trees in late summer to eat moths — flipping rocks to get at them and putting away up to 40,000 in a day, which is most of a year's fat in a few weeks.
animals.role: The biggest thing on the mountain and the reason everything else stays alert. It digs whole slopes apart for roots and ground squirrels, which turns the soil over, and in late summer it climbs above the trees to eat moths off the rockslides. It will drive a wolverine off a carcass without breaking stride.

requirements.hint: A high open slope soft enough to dig, rocks to flip for moths, and a mountain already full enough to feed something this big.

animals.name: Grasshopper Mouse
animals.diet: scorpions, centipedes, beetles and other mice
animals.shelter: Takes over a burrow another animal dug, then defends it
animals.preferredHabitat: Open sandy flats with scattered brush and plenty of prey underfoot
animals.fact: This mouse hunts scorpions, gets stung in the face, and carries on eating — its body turns the venom's pain signal off. Then it stands up on its hind legs and howls at the moon like a tiny wolf.
animals.role: A mouse that decided to be a predator. It keeps scorpions and big insects in check, and it is one of the only animals that can eat the desert's most venomous residents without flinching.

requirements.hint: An old burrow it can take over and open ground to hunt across. It gets all its water from what it catches.

animals.name: Snow Bunting
animals.diet: seeds blown onto the snow, plus insects in the short summer
animals.shelter: Deep in a rock crevice, lined with feathers and fur against the cold
animals.preferredHabitat: Windswept ridges and fellfield where the snow blows clear
animals.fact: Snow buntings nest further north than any other songbird on Earth, tucked so deep in rock cracks that the male has to feed the female in the dark while she sits.
animals.role: A small bird that treats a blizzard as ordinary weather. Flocks drift across bare ridges picking up seed the wind has stranded on the snow, and they turn from white to warm brown as the season turns.

requirements.hint: A deep, dry crack in the rock out of the wind, and open stony ground nearby where the snow blows clear.

animals.name: Groundhog
animals.diet: grass, clover, dandelions and just about any tender green thing it can reach
animals.shelter: A burrow with several entrances, a grass-lined sleeping chamber and a separate toilet room
animals.preferredHabitat: Meadow edges with deep, well-drained soil it can tunnel through
animals.fact: A groundhog digs a burrow with a front door, a back door, a bedroom and a separate room for going to the toilet — and moves about a tonne of soil doing it. In winter its heart slows to about five beats a minute.
animals.role: The meadow's earthmover. Its abandoned burrows become homes for foxes, snakes, rabbits and half the small animals here, so one groundhog's digging outlives the groundhog by years.

requirements.hint: Deep, well-drained soil at the edge of the grass, with a bolt-hole close by. It wants somewhere to dig more than somewhere to hide.

animals.name: Opossum
animals.diet: almost anything — insects, fruit, eggs, carrion, and an enormous number of ticks
animals.shelter: Sleeps the day out in a hollow log or a borrowed burrow, and rarely uses the same one twice
animals.preferredHabitat: Brushy edges with hollow wood, water nearby and plenty to scavenge
animals.fact: When an opossum plays dead it is not acting — it faints. The body goes stiff, the tongue lolls out and it gives off a smell like something long dead, and it cannot snap out of it for several minutes even if you walk away.
animals.role: The meadow's clean-up crew. It eats what everything else has left, including carrion and vast quantities of ticks, and it is the only animal here that carries its young around on its back.

requirements.hint: Hollow wood to sleep the day away in and berries within a night's walk. It moves house constantly, so give it more than one option.

animals.name: Song Sparrow
animals.diet: insects and spiders in summer; seeds, berries and grass heads the rest of the year
animals.shelter: A cup of grass tucked low in a shrub or a thick tussock, close to damp ground
animals.preferredHabitat: Brushy, slightly damp edges — the messy strip between open grass and thicker cover
animals.fact: Every song sparrow makes up its own tunes. A young male listens to the neighbours, then invents his own set of eight or ten and sings them for life, so you can learn to tell individual birds apart by ear.
animals.role: One of the first birds to find a mending meadow and one of the last to leave it. It works the scruffy middle ground, eating insects all summer and switching to seeds in winter.

requirements.hint: A damp, messy corner with a thick tussock to hide a nest in and berries close by. It likes the untidy bits best.
