habitatObjects.name: Grass Patch
habitatObjects.description: A soft patch of regrowing grass. A first step for any bare ground.

habitatObjects.name: Native Grass Patch
habitatObjects.description: Deep-rooted native bunchgrass that sends roots down further than it stands tall. It holds soil together and keeps the ground covered year-round.

habitatObjects.name: Wildflower Patch
habitatObjects.description: Mixed native wildflowers in a loose, unplanned drift. A wide splash of colour you can pick out from a long way off.

habitatObjects.name: Poppy Patch
habitatObjects.description: Field poppies, an old European farm weed. Lovely in a garden bed; they are not part of a native prairie planting.

habitatObjects.name: Sunflower Patch
habitatObjects.description: Tall common sunflowers (Helianthus annuus), a true North American native, left standing through the autumn instead of cut back — the seed heads dry hard on the stalk and stay put.

habitatObjects.name: Lupine Patch
habitatObjects.description: Spires of blue lupine that fix the soil as they bloom.

habitatObjects.name: Willow Tree
habitatObjects.description: The preserve's namesake — a graceful willow grown from a watered bed.

habitatObjects.name: Oak Tree
habitatObjects.description: An acorn-grown oak. Slow at first, and then for decades the most productive single tree you can put in the ground — nothing else in North America supports as much.

habitatObjects.name: Pine Tree
habitatObjects.description: A young pine grown from a cone — evergreen shelter in any season.

habitatObjects.name: Butterfly Flowers
habitatObjects.description: A mixed bed of native nectar flowers — blazing star, aster and bee balm — chosen so something is open from midsummer right through autumn. Milkweed is now its own plant and has to be sown separately.

habitatObjects.name: Pollinator Garden
habitatObjects.description: A dense bed of overlapping bloom, planned so that something is always open from the first warm week to the last. Nectar and pollen, all season, in one place.

habitatObjects.name: Shrub
habitatObjects.description: A young native shrub — quick, dense cover at knee height. But a meadow is a grassland, and letting shrubs spread across it turns it into something else entirely.

habitatObjects.name: Berry Bush
habitatObjects.description: A native thimbleberry and wild rose thicket — prickly, as most native brambles are, and heavy with fruit by late summer. Sow it in a watered bed from seeds and a few berries.

habitatObjects.name: Small Pond
habitatObjects.description: A clay-lined pond. Clean drinking water changes everything.

habitatObjects.name: Woodland Pool
habitatObjects.description: A shaded forest pool fed by a cold spring. Deep shade, cold clean water, and a soft muddy edge you can walk right down to.

habitatObjects.name: Fern Spring
habitatObjects.description: A mossy seep ringed with ferns — damp ground that wakes the whole understory.

habitatObjects.name: Shallow Water Pool
habitatObjects.description: A gently sloped pool with a long sunlit shallow edge you could wade across without wetting your knees. Shallow and warm rather than deep — no substitute for real depth.

habitatObjects.name: Log Shelter
habitatObjects.description: Fallen logs stacked into a loose pile, with gaps running right through the middle. Damp underneath, and slowly going soft.

habitatObjects.name: Hollow Log
habitatObjects.description: A fallen log carefully opened out down the middle into a dry, close chamber with an entrance at one end.

habitatObjects.name: Rock Pile
habitatObjects.description: Flat stones piled loosely so the sun bakes the top while the gaps underneath stay cool and damp.

habitatObjects.name: Fallen Branch Shelter
habitatObjects.description: A loose pile of branches thrown together rather than stacked, twigs and all. Humble, and riddled with gaps to disappear into.

habitatObjects.name: Bird Perch
habitatObjects.description: A tall bare snag with a clear view in every direction and open sky above it.

habitatObjects.name: Stepping-Stone Path
habitatObjects.description: Flat stepping stones that keep your boots off the new growth.

habitatObjects.name: Gravel Path
habitatObjects.description: Crunchy gravel underfoot — keeps boots off the new growth.

habitatObjects.name: Plank Path
habitatObjects.description: Weathered boardwalk planks, kind to soft ground.

habitatObjects.name: Flagstone Path
habitatObjects.description: Broad flat stones set into the earth.

habitatObjects.name: Mossy Path
habitatObjects.description: Old stones wearing soft green moss — they keep boots off the wet ground without compacting it.

habitatObjects.name: Wooden Bridge
habitatObjects.description: A sturdy plank bridge — place it over a pond or wet swale so boots stay off the soft ground.

habitatObjects.name: Wooden Fence
habitatObjects.description: A low rail fence that marks quiet zones for recovering ground.

habitatObjects.name: Nesting Tree
habitatObjects.description: A fast-growing native sapling. Give it a few seasons and it will be tall enough to hold weight in its crown.

habitatObjects.name: Standing Deadwood
habitatObjects.description: A dead snag left standing and safely anchored. The bigger around it is the better — a slim stub is easy to work, but only a full trunk can hold anything large.

habitatObjects.name: Mushroom Log
habitatObjects.description: A damp, mossy log seeded with fungi. The fungus is doing the real work — it digests the wood, which is what turns a dead log into food, soil and shelter for everything else.

habitatObjects.name: Reed Bed
habitatObjects.description: Dense replanted reeds standing in shallow water, thick enough to walk into and lose sight of the bank.

habitatObjects.name: Mud Bank
habitatObjects.description: A shaped bank of bare, soft, damp earth sloping down into the water, open to the sun and easy to dig. Requires the restoration shovel.

habitatObjects.name: Nesting Platform
habitatObjects.description: A raised, quiet platform out in the open with a broad flat top and nothing overhanging it. It is not a substitute for a tree cavity, a bank tunnel or a colony rookery.

habitatObjects.name: Cattail Stand
habitatObjects.description: Tall cattails crowded along the water's edge — dense at the base, and shading the shallows behind them.

habitatObjects.name: Marsh Log
habitatObjects.description: A half-sunken log, one end up in the sun and the other lost under water. Dark, close gaps run beneath it the whole way.

habitatObjects.name: Lily Pool
habitatObjects.description: Still, clean water blanketed edge to edge with lily pads, with cool shaded water underneath them.

habitatObjects.name: Burrow Mound
habitatObjects.description: A heaped mound of loose, well-drained earth with one bare face, soft enough to tunnel straight into. Requires the restoration shovel.

habitatObjects.name: Cactus Patch
habitatObjects.description: Transplanted native pad and barrel cactus. Fruit, moisture and a spiny fortress in one — though nothing this short can hold a cavity.

habitatObjects.name: Desert Brush
habitatObjects.description: A mixed stand of bursage and brittlebush — the low scrub that fills the gaps between the bigger shrubs.

habitatObjects.name: Shaded Rock Shelter
habitatObjects.description: Stacked slabs with a cool dark gap — shelter from the midday sun.

habitatObjects.name: Alpine Wildflower Patch
habitatObjects.description: Tough little high-country forbs, low and tight to the ground, flowering all at once in the short summer. Nectar, seed and green leaf — forage, not shelter.

habitatObjects.name: Snowmelt Pool
habitatObjects.description: A stone-lined pool that catches cold, clean snowmelt and holds it clear. Leave it unstocked — high alpine water was naturally barren, and what gets put into it does not come out again.

habitatObjects.name: Tidepool
habitatObjects.description: A restored rocky pool that keeps a pocket of the sea behind when the tide drops. Only ever a pocket — it warms, it goes salty, and it waits.

habitatObjects.name: Dune Grass
habitatObjects.description: Native American dunegrass (Leymus mollis), which holds blowing sand in open, patchy clumps rather than a dense wall.

habitatObjects.name: Driftwood Shelter
habitatObjects.description: Weathered driftwood stacked into beach shelter.

habitatObjects.name: Kelp Wrack
habitatObjects.description: A protected line of washed-up kelp left lying where the tide dropped it, going soft and dark underneath. Groom it away and the beach loses the only real food it gets.

habitatObjects.name: Coastal Nesting Area
habitatObjects.description: A general roped-off stretch of quiet upper beach, marked with posts and line. It protects the ground broadly — the narrower closures are far more particular about what they cover.

habitatObjects.name: Coral Garden
habitatObjects.description: DEPRECATED — do not offer in this biome. There are no shallow reef-building corals in the temperate northeast Pacific; reef corals need water around 23-25 C and this coast runs 11-21 C. Replaced by the Kelp Forest object.

habitatObjects.name: Sea Glass Lantern
habitatObjects.description: Beach-found glass set into a driftwood frame — it throws soft sea-green light at dusk.

habitatObjects.name: Tide Chime
habitatObjects.description: Shells and sea glass strung on driftwood that ring softly in the onshore breeze.

habitatObjects.name: Pearl Display
habitatObjects.description: A polished shell cradle for beachcombed treasures. Note: there is no natural pearl fishery on this coast, and taking live shellfish for pearls is not restoration — display only what the tide gave up.

habitatObjects.name: Sea Glass Path
habitatObjects.description: Tumbled sea glass pressed into the sand — a glittering walkway that keeps boots off the dunes.

habitatObjects.name: Small Chest
habitatObjects.description: A woven-and-wood chest. Holds 120 materials. Anything stored here feeds crafting from anywhere.

habitatObjects.name: Medium Chest
habitatObjects.description: A sturdier chest. Holds 250 materials.

habitatObjects.name: Field Journal Stand
habitatObjects.description: A little lectern for your field journal — read it anywhere you place one.

habitatObjects.name: Potted Flowers
habitatObjects.description: A clay pot of meadow flowers to brighten your camp.

habitatObjects.name: Wetland Restoration Kit
habitatObjects.description: Liners, filters, and channel tools — everything needed to re-water the wetland. Crafting it helps unlock Rushwater Wetland.

habitatObjects.name: Migration Path Marker
habitatObjects.description: Cairns and markers that restore a safe migration path through the heights. Crafting it helps unlock Pelican Shore.

habitatObjects.name: Forest Restoration Kit
habitatObjects.description: Seed mixes, fiber twine, and trail tools to open the overgrown forest path. Crafting it helps unlock Old Hollow Forest.

habitatObjects.name: Scrubland Restoration Kit
habitatObjects.description: Sediment sleds and hardy cuttings to carry restoration into the dry scrubland. Crafting it helps unlock Redstone Scrubland.

habitatObjects.name: Alpine Restoration Kit
habitatObjects.description: Shade cloth, water caches, and climbing gear for the high country. Crafting it helps unlock Graywind Heights.

habitatObjects.name: Stone Lantern
habitatObjects.description: A little stone lantern with a warm glow to light the path.

habitatObjects.name: Wooden Bench
habitatObjects.description: A weathered bench, silvered by salt and sun — a quiet place to sit for a long while and just look.

habitatObjects.name: Garden Arch
habitatObjects.description: A flowering arch that frames a path, heavy with bloom by midsummer. Pretty, but it is a garden feature rather than habitat, and nothing here depends on one.

habitatObjects.name: Bird Bath
habitatObjects.description: A shallow stone basin on a pedestal, no deeper than a thumb, with a rough bottom for footing and fresh water in it.

habitatObjects.name: Trail Signpost
habitatObjects.description: A hand-painted signpost to guide visitors through the preserve.

habitatObjects.name: Planter Box
habitatObjects.description: A timber box planted with desert natives — brittlebush, penstemon and globemallow rather than garden flowers.

habitatObjects.name: Gazebo
habitatObjects.description: A roofed open-air pavilion — a charming centerpiece and a shady spot to watch the preserve.

habitatObjects.name: Clover Patch
habitatObjects.description: Introduced clover and birdsfoot trefoil, soft and green underfoot. It crowds out native forbs — treat it as a garden patch, not restoration.

habitatObjects.name: Brush Pile
habitatObjects.description: A loose pile of branches, thickest at the bottom and open through the middle, with runs and gaps at ground level.

habitatObjects.name: Fern Grove
habitatObjects.description: Shady arching ferns that carpet the forest floor.

habitatObjects.name: Tree Stump
habitatObjects.description: A mossy old stump riddled with holes and soft rot, crumbling a little further into the ground every year.

habitatObjects.name: Sedge Tussock
habitatObjects.description: Clumped sedges standing in the shallows, each one a dense knee-high tuft with dry footing in the middle of it.

habitatObjects.name: Alder Snag
habitatObjects.description: A standing dead alder drowned by rising water, its trunk riddled with old cavities and its bare top branches reaching out over open water.

habitatObjects.name: Agave Rosette
habitatObjects.description: A spiny rosette that spends years low to the ground and then throws up a single flowering mast taller than you are.

habitatObjects.name: Ocotillo
habitatObjects.description: Whip-like stalks with crimson tips — cover and nectar in the open flats.

habitatObjects.name: Heather Mat
habitatObjects.description: A low alpine mat of heather blossoms above the talus.

habitatObjects.name: Krummholz Pine
habitatObjects.description: A wind-sculpted dwarf pine — rare shelter at the tree line.

habitatObjects.name: Eelgrass Bed
habitatObjects.description: Swaying eelgrass (Zostera marina) rooted in soft mud in a sheltered bay — an underwater meadow, dense enough to disappear into.

habitatObjects.name: Oyster Bed
habitatObjects.description: A restored reef of native Olympia oysters (Ostrea lurida) — the Pacific coast's own oyster and a real restoration target, not the introduced Pacific oyster.

habitatObjects.name: Daisy Patch
habitatObjects.description: Oxeye daisies — pretty, but introduced from Europe and listed as a noxious weed in several places. Cheerful decoration, not native meadow restoration.

habitatObjects.name: Foxglove
habitatObjects.description: Foxglove — introduced, poisonous in every part, and invasive in some regions. Decorative only.

habitatObjects.name: Mushroom Ring
habitatObjects.description: A fairy ring of woodland mushrooms in the leaf litter.

habitatObjects.name: Birch Tree
habitatObjects.description: A slender white-barked birch grown from a watered bed.

habitatObjects.name: Marsh Marigold
habitatObjects.description: Golden marsh marigolds ringing the seepy shallows in spring, out before almost anything else. A reliable sign that the wet-meadow edge is working.

habitatObjects.name: Bulrush
habitatObjects.description: Stately bulrushes with brown velvet heads along the bank.

habitatObjects.name: Prickly Pear
habitatObjects.description: Pad cactus with sweet fruit and bright blooms.

habitatObjects.name: Desert Marigold
habitatObjects.description: Drought-tough marigolds that glow against the sand.

habitatObjects.name: Alpine Gentian
habitatObjects.description: Vivid blue alpine gentians, low against the wind.

habitatObjects.name: Moss Cushion
habitatObjects.description: A springy cushion of moss campion and alpine avens, tight as upholstery and noticeably warm and damp inside.

habitatObjects.name: Sea Thrift
habitatObjects.description: Pink sea-thrift pompoms that thrive in salt spray.

habitatObjects.name: Beach Shrub
habitatObjects.description: A salt-hardy grey-green coastal scrub of the back dune and bluff, wind-pruned flat on top and dense underneath.

habitatObjects.name: Nectar Feeder
habitatObjects.description: A sugar-water feeder on a hook. Pretty, and fun to watch — but sugar water is not food, so treat this as decoration rather than habitat.

habitatObjects.name: Crystal Cairn
habitatObjects.description: A cracked geode set on stacked stones — a glittering desert landmark.

habitatObjects.name: Sun Totem
habitatObjects.description: A carved sandstone totem crowned with a desert crystal.

habitatObjects.name: Palo Verde Tree
habitatObjects.description: The green-barked desert tree — rare shade and yellow blooms for the scrubland.

habitatObjects.name: Shore Pine
habitatObjects.description: A salt-bent pine, low and broad, that anchors the back dunes and breaks the wind coming off the water.

habitatObjects.name: Bald Cypress
habitatObjects.description: A towering swamp cypress with a flared, knee-rooted base — a southeastern bottomland tree, planted here as an ornamental. It is outside its natural range in a northern emergent marsh.

habitatObjects.name: Water Tupelo
habitatObjects.description: A round-crowned wetland tree whose swollen base stands in the water — a southeastern bottomland species, planted here as an ornamental and outside its natural range.

habitatObjects.name: Mesquite
habitatObjects.description: A low, spreading desert tree — airy shade and seed pods for the scrubland.

habitatObjects.name: Desert Ironwood
habitatObjects.description: A dense, slow-growing ironwood — a vital nurse tree in the open desert.

habitatObjects.name: Subalpine Fir
habitatObjects.description: A slender spire fir that shrugs off the high-country snow.

habitatObjects.name: Quaking Aspen
habitatObjects.description: White-barked aspen whose golden leaves shiver in the wind. It grows in sheltered subalpine basins well below the tundra, never above treeline.

habitatObjects.name: Monterey Cypress
habitatObjects.description: A wind-flattened coastal cypress sculpted by the sea breeze — planted here, not native: wild Monterey cypress survives in only two relict groves on the Monterey Peninsula.

habitatObjects.name: Coast Live Oak
habitatObjects.description: A broad evergreen oak that anchors the back shore with deep shade.

habitatObjects.name: Campfire
habitatObjects.description: A crackling campfire ringed with stones — the heart of camp.

habitatObjects.name: String Lights
habitatObjects.description: A string of warm little lanterns to hang over your camp.

habitatObjects.name: Pinwheel
habitatObjects.description: A bright pinwheel that spins in the breeze.

habitatObjects.name: Birdhouse
habitatObjects.description: A hand-built birdhouse on a post — charming, even when empty.

habitatObjects.name: Flower Cart
habitatObjects.description: A little wooden cart overflowing with cut flowers.

habitatObjects.name: Hammock
habitatObjects.description: A woven hammock strung between two posts for lazy afternoons.

habitatObjects.name: Garden Gnome
habitatObjects.description: A cheerful little gnome to watch over the garden.

habitatObjects.name: Wind Chimes
habitatObjects.description: Driftwood chimes that sing softly when the wind moves through.

habitatObjects.name: Sundial
habitatObjects.description: A carved stone sundial for telling time the slow way.

habitatObjects.name: Stone Cairn
habitatObjects.description: A balanced stack of smooth stones marking a quiet spot.

habitatObjects.name: Picnic Blanket
habitatObjects.description: A checked blanket spread out for a sunny picnic.

habitatObjects.name: Flower Pot Row
habitatObjects.description: A tidy row of terracotta pots brimming with blooms.

habitatObjects.name: Insect Hotel
habitatObjects.description: A stack of hollow and pithy stems, drilled blocks and bark riddled with old boring holes, packed into a frame under a small roof. Tubes of every width, from pencil-thin down to a hair.

habitatObjects.name: Dry Stone Wall
habitatObjects.description: A low wall of stacked stones laid without mortar, cool and shady in the gaps between them.

habitatObjects.name: Bat Box
habitatObjects.description: A tall, narrow wooden box with a rough inner face and an open slot along the bottom, mounted high and facing the sun. The gap inside is barely wider than a finger.

habitatObjects.name: Leaf Litter Pile
habitatObjects.description: A mound of damp leaves and moss left where it fell, warm in the middle and slowly turning to soil.

habitatObjects.name: Duck Nest Box
habitatObjects.description: A raised wooden box on a pole standing over water, with a round entrance high on one face and a bed of wood shavings inside.

habitatObjects.name: Basking Log
habitatObjects.description: A half-submerged log angled up out of the water into full sun, dry along its upper length and slick below. Getting properly warm out here is not a luxury.

habitatObjects.name: Rock Crevice
habitatObjects.description: Stacked slabs leaving narrow shady cracks that run back further than you can see, cool even at midday.

habitatObjects.name: Dew Basin
habitatObjects.description: A shallow clay basin that catches dew and rain — precious desert water.

habitatObjects.name: Talus Pile
habitatObjects.description: A jumble of broken rock with deep spaces between the blocks — runways and hollows running right down into the pile.

habitatObjects.name: Nest Shelf
habitatObjects.description: A sheltered rock ledge lined with moss, out of the wind and with a solid overhang above it.

habitatObjects.name: Driftwood Pile
habitatObjects.description: A tangle of sun-bleached driftwood, silver-grey and hollow-sounding, with damp shade under the lowest pieces.

habitatObjects.name: Nesting Bluff
habitatObjects.description: A built-up sandy bank with narrow ledges cut across its face, sheer below and out of reach from the ground.

habitatObjects.name: Pika Haypile
habitatObjects.description: A stockpile of grasses and flowers cut green and cured dry under a rock overhang, packed tight and out of the rain.

habitatObjects.name: Lichen Boulder
habitatObjects.description: A weathered boulder crusted with map lichen. It grows roughly a millimetre every ten years, quietly crumbling the rock into the first grains of alpine soil.

habitatObjects.name: Scree Slope
habitatObjects.description: A shifting apron of shattered rock, laced with the runways and hideaways of the high country.

habitatObjects.name: Snowbank Roost
habitatObjects.description: A packed drift of late-lying snow, firm enough on top to walk on and soft enough underneath to push into. Inside a drift like this the wind stops entirely.

habitatObjects.name: Whitebark Seed Cache
habitatObjects.description: A hidden larder of whitebark pine nuts buried a few centimetres down — rich, oily seed, kept sound right through the winter.

habitatObjects.name: Juniper Thicket
habitatObjects.description: A low, hardy juniper heavy with frosted berries — cover and winter food where little else grows.

habitatObjects.name: Cliff Nest Niche
habitatObjects.description: A sheltered cleft in the cliff face, mossed and tucked back out of sight, dry under an overhanging lip.

habitatObjects.name: Crystal Snowmelt Spring
habitatObjects.description: An ice-cold spring welling up through quartz — the purest, coldest water in the heights.

habitatObjects.name: Summit Prayer Flags
habitatObjects.description: A bright line of weatherworn flags strung between cairns, snapping in the alpine wind.

habitatObjects.name: Quartz Lantern
habitatObjects.description: A stone lantern set with a glowing shard of quartz that holds the last of the daylight.

habitatObjects.name: Obsidian Totem
habitatObjects.description: A polished column of volcanic glass that catches the high light like dark, still water.

habitatObjects.name: Large Chest
habitatObjects.description: A big iron-banded storage chest. Holds 500 materials — your main stockpile.

habitatObjects.name: Woven Rug
habitatObjects.description: A soft woven rug to warm the floor of your home.

habitatObjects.name: Little Table
habitatObjects.description: A small wooden table with a sprig of flowers.

habitatObjects.name: Cozy Bed
habitatObjects.description: A comfortable bed for resting between restoration days.

habitatObjects.name: Bookshelf
habitatObjects.description: A shelf of field guides and well-thumbed nature books.

habitatObjects.name: Cozy Armchair
habitatObjects.description: A plush armchair to sink into after a long day's restoring.

habitatObjects.name: Stone Fireplace
habitatObjects.description: A crackling stone hearth that warms the whole room.

habitatObjects.name: Floor Lamp
habitatObjects.description: A soft floor lamp for cozy evenings indoors.

habitatObjects.name: House Plant
habitatObjects.description: A leafy potted plant to bring a little of the meadow inside.

habitatObjects.name: Framed Landscape
habitatObjects.description: A framed painting of the preserve at its finest.

habitatObjects.name: Sleeping Bag
habitatObjects.description: A simple sleeping bag — just the thing for a cozy night in the tent.

habitatObjects.name: Floor Cushions
habitatObjects.description: A pile of soft floor cushions for lounging.

habitatObjects.name: Wooden Stool
habitatObjects.description: A simple cushioned stool.

habitatObjects.name: Mushroom Shelf
habitatObjects.description: A little shelf dotted with woodland mushrooms.

habitatObjects.name: Reed Floor Mat
habitatObjects.description: A woven reed mat from the marsh.

habitatObjects.name: Potted Cactus
habitatObjects.description: A hardy little cactus in a clay pot.

habitatObjects.name: Driftwood Shelf
habitatObjects.description: A shelf of weathered driftwood with beach finds.

habitatObjects.name: Wall Clock
habitatObjects.description: A handsome wall clock — a house needs one.

habitatObjects.name: Wooden Dresser
habitatObjects.description: A sturdy chest of drawers.

habitatObjects.name: Woolly Rug
habitatObjects.description: A thick, warm rug for cold mountain nights.

habitatObjects.name: Antler Chandelier
habitatObjects.description: A grand candle chandelier — fit for a lodge.

habitatObjects.name: Aquarium
habitatObjects.description: A glass tank of darting little fish.

habitatObjects.name: Stargazing Telescope
habitatObjects.description: A brass telescope for the clear mountain sky.

habitatObjects.name: Rain Basin
habitatObjects.description: A carved stone bowl that catches rainwater and holds it. Precious out here, and rarely full for long.

habitatObjects.name: Dewlit Lantern
habitatObjects.description: Decoration. A glass globe of glowing morning dew that throws a soft green light — invented, not habitat.

habitatObjects.name: Sunstone Cairn
habitatObjects.description: Decoration. A stack of sun-baked stones that hold the day's warmth long into the cool evening — pretty, but nothing here actually needs one.

habitatObjects.name: Frostflower Planter
habitatObjects.description: Decoration. A planter of imaginary pale ice-blooms — a made-up flower, not a plant you could grow.

habitatObjects.name: Stormglass Lantern
habitatObjects.description: A shard of lightning-fused glass that flickers with a cold inner light.

habitatObjects.name: Frostflower Vase
habitatObjects.description: A glass vase of ice-blooms for the windowsill — they never wilt.

habitatObjects.name: Stormglass Chandelier
habitatObjects.description: A hanging cluster of lightning-glass shards that scatters cool light across the room.

habitatObjects.name: Marsh Boardwalk
habitatObjects.description: A raised plank walkway. Nothing out here needs one — it exists so that you don't: every footstep off it compacts mud, crushes stems and opens a path straight through cover.

habitatObjects.name: Heron Rookery
habitatObjects.description: A stand of tall snags and crowns carrying a dozen bulky stick platforms, all within sight of one another. A rookery is a colony, not a single structure — one platform on its own is not the same thing.

habitatObjects.name: Dragonfly Pond
habitatObjects.description: A clear pool ringed with reeds — open sunlit water in the middle, and stems running from the bottom right up past the surface.

habitatObjects.name: Trail Tent
habitatObjects.description: A snug canvas tent you can step inside and decorate — a little home base away from home. Pitch one in each wild biome beyond the meadow.

habitatObjects.name: Headlamp
habitatObjects.description: A hand-wound lamp on a woven strap. Once crafted it's yours for good — after dusk, a warm beam lights the ground around you wherever you roam.

habitatObjects.name: Field Binoculars
habitatObjects.description: Hand-ground lenses in a woven grip. Once crafted they're yours for good — animals you haven't recorded in your journal yet catch the light with a soft glint.

habitatObjects.name: Hiking Boots
habitatObjects.description: Sturdy boots cobbled from tough forest bark, springy moss, and woven wetland reeds. Once crafted they're yours for good — wear them to roam the preserve a little faster.

habitatObjects.name: Fellfield Gravel
habitatObjects.description: Wind-scoured gravel that freezes, heaves and re-sorts itself every spring, held together by thin crusts of lichen. It looks like nothing, and it is the only ground a cushion plant will take.

habitatObjects.name: Alpine Turf Mat
habitatObjects.description: A knitted mat of sedge, alpine avens and cushion plants over dark alpine soil. Turf like this takes decades to close over bare ground, and one summer of boot traffic to open it up again.

habitatObjects.name: Snowmelt Litter Mat
habitatObjects.description: A sodden mat of last year's stems and leaves, released as the snowpack pulls back. Almost all of the alpine's decomposition happens in these few damp weeks.

habitatObjects.name: Rotting Conifer Log
habitatObjects.description: A well-rotted subalpine fir log lying where the drifts pile deepest, soft enough to push a finger into. Dead wood is habitat, not mess.

habitatObjects.name: Escape Cliff
habitatObjects.description: A near-vertical band of broken cliff, cut with ledges and footholds the whole way up. Nothing can be cornered on ground like this.

habitatObjects.name: Willow Basin Thicket
habitatObjects.description: Planeleaf and snow willow filling a sheltered basin, low and dense and buried by drifts each winter. Its buds and twigs stay reachable when everything else this high is under snow.

habitatObjects.name: Boulder Burrow Den
habitatObjects.description: A deep, many-chambered burrow tunnelled under a boulder, well below the frost line. Down there the temperature barely moves all winter.

habitatObjects.name: Inherited Earth Den
habitatObjects.description: A hollow opened up under boulders and roots by whoever dug it first, then widened and taken over. Second-hand, and none the worse for it.

habitatObjects.name: Stonecrop Patch
habitatObjects.description: Lance-leaved stonecrop wedged into gravel and rock cracks, its fat leaves storing water where there is almost no soil. Nothing else in the high country substitutes for it.

habitatObjects.name: Nest Burrow
habitatObjects.description: An abandoned tunnel in the turf, packed with dry grass and old bedding — a ready-made cavity, warm and dark, that nobody had to dig.

habitatObjects.name: Chipmunk Burrow Larder
habitatObjects.description: A shallow tunnel under a slab with a side chamber packed full of seed heads, dry and reachable all winter. No species in the game requires it any more.

habitatObjects.name: Whitebark Pine
habitatObjects.description: A whitebark pine grown from a seed buried and never dug back up. Its cones do not open on their own, so it cannot spread anywhere without help.

habitatObjects.name: Old Woodpecker Cavity
habitatObjects.description: A round chiselled hole in a dead trunk, cut seasons ago and left empty since. The entrance is still clean-edged and the chamber below is dry.

habitatObjects.name: Snowfield Debris Line
habitatObjects.description: The dark seam of wind-carried seed, pollen and grit stranded along the edge of a shrinking snowfield — a free delivery, carried uphill and dropped.

habitatObjects.name: Toad Upland Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A borrowed tunnel in damp ground above a breeding pool, below the frost line and above the water table. Somewhere to sit out eight months of the year.

habitatObjects.name: Treeline Log Den
habitatObjects.description: A hollow log at the edge of the last trees, buried by drifts all winter, with tunnels running away from it under the snowpack.

habitatObjects.name: Fur-Lined Prey Den
habitatObjects.description: A stolen burrow, relined with fur from whatever dug it. Small, close and warm — and no work at all to move into.

habitatObjects.name: Cliff Eyrie
habitatObjects.description: A bulky stick eyrie on a sheer ledge, added to year after year until the same pair has used it for decades.

habitatObjects.name: Ledge Den
habitatObjects.description: A dry overhang deep in broken cliff, screened by fallen rock. Invisible from below, and reachable only along one narrow ledge.

habitatObjects.name: Krummholz Bed Hollow
habitatObjects.description: A shaded, wind-broken scrape pressed flat into the ground under the krummholz. Out of the sun, out of the wind, and out of sight from above.

habitatObjects.name: Kelp Holdfast Reef
habitatObjects.description: Clean rock on the shallow seafloor for kelp holdfasts to grip. Kelp is not rooted in sand — without hard bottom the whole forest washes away.

habitatObjects.name: Upwelling Current
habitatObjects.description: Cold, nutrient-rich water rising from the deep along the shore. It is the fertiliser of this whole coast — everything here is ultimately running on it.

habitatObjects.name: Coralline Turf
habitatObjects.description: Pink, branching coralline and red algae turf on low-zone rock. Surfgrass seeds carry bristly arms that hook onto these branches — no turf, no surfgrass.

habitatObjects.name: Low-Tide Rock Bench
habitatObjects.description: A broad shelf of bedrock uncovered only at the lowest tides — the richest strip of the shore, and the one that is underwater most of the time.

habitatObjects.name: Urchin Pit
habitatObjects.description: Rounded hollows ground into solid rock, each a smooth bowl about a hand's width across. Once a pit like this is started it only ever gets deeper.

habitatObjects.name: Kelp Forest
habitatObjects.description: Living giant kelp rising from the seafloor to a golden canopy at the surface. Dim green water the whole way up, and fronds thick enough to lie back in.

habitatObjects.name: Surfgrass Bed
habitatObjects.description: A green meadow of surfgrass streaming out in the surge on low-zone rock, so dense you cannot see the stone underneath.

habitatObjects.name: Nearshore Spawning Shallows
habitatObjects.description: Quiet, plankton-rich water just off the surf line, barely moving and thick with drifting food. Warm at the top, and calm enough that nothing sinks in a hurry.

habitatObjects.name: Open Sand Beach
habitatObjects.description: Wide, flat, unplanted sand above the tide line. Bare open sand is habitat in its own right here — leave the sight lines long and the surface undisturbed.

habitatObjects.name: Empty Shell Drift
habitatObjects.description: A pocket of empty shells caught in a rock hollow, sorted by the waves and heaped up by size. A beach with no spare shells on it is missing something.

habitatObjects.name: Subtidal Rubble Flat
habitatObjects.description: Loose cobble and broken rock just below the tide, where dead material drifts in and settles down between the stones.

habitatObjects.name: Surge-Swept Rock Face
habitatObjects.description: Open rock taking the full weight of the swell. Punishing to hold onto, and the water never stops moving past it.

habitatObjects.name: Barnacle Crust
habitatObjects.description: A white crust of acorn barnacles welded across the upper rock — sharp underfoot, rough as coarse sandpaper, and cemented on so hard it is part of the stone.

habitatObjects.name: Sheltered Sand-Gravel Flat
habitatObjects.description: Stable mixed sand and gravel in the lee of a headland — firm enough to dig into and calm enough that it stays exactly where it is.

habitatObjects.name: Muddy Seabed
habitatObjects.description: Soft, deep sediment along the kelp edge, so thick with tube-building amphipods that the seafloor is more animal than mud.

habitatObjects.name: Sheltered Cobble Field
habitatObjects.description: Loose stones lying on a shore the surf never reaches hard, each one damp and dark underneath. The underside is the habitat, not the top.

habitatObjects.name: Splash-Zone Crevice
habitatObjects.description: Dry-looking cracks in rock that the waves only ever reach as spray. The highest, driest tier of the shore — salt, sun, and hardly any water at all.

habitatObjects.name: Shell-Dropping Rock
habitatObjects.description: A flat, hard-topped boulder standing clear of the sand, scattered with cracked shells. Hard enough that anything dropped on it from a height breaks open.

habitatObjects.name: Swash-Zone Runnel
habitatObjects.description: The wet, sliding strip where each wave runs out and drains back again, turning the top few centimetres of sand over with every surge.

habitatObjects.name: Plover Scrape Closure
habitatObjects.description: A roped-off stretch of bare, open, unvegetated sand with symbolic fencing and signs. There is nothing to build here — what protects the ground is that nobody walks across it.

habitatObjects.name: High-Tide Roost
habitatObjects.description: A raised rock or islet that stays dry even at the top of the tide, with open water all around it. Somewhere to stand and wait out the hours when the flats are gone.

habitatObjects.name: Dune Manzanita
habitatObjects.description: Low sandmat manzanita, a coastal dune shrub that flowers in midwinter and holds its berries hard into the cold months — food behind the beach exactly when there is nothing else going.

habitatObjects.name: Mussel Bed
habitatObjects.description: A dense band of blue-black mussels layered two and three deep across mid-zone rock, packed so tight the shells hold each other upright. The gaps between them run right down to the stone.

habitatObjects.name: Sunlit Surge Pool
habitatObjects.description: A deep pool flushed by every wave and open straight to the sky — surge pouring food down from the rocks above, and full sun reaching all the way to the bottom.

habitatObjects.name: Offshore Nesting Island
habitatObjects.description: A rock stack or islet standing off the coast, with deep water all around and no way onto it on foot. Nothing that walks can reach it.

habitatObjects.name: Sandbar Roost
habitatObjects.description: A low sandbar that dries out between tides — flat, open, ringed with water, and far enough off the beach to be left alone.

habitatObjects.name: Seal Haul-Out Rocks
habitatObjects.description: Low rocks and a sand spit with a wide buffer of quiet kept around them, sloping gently enough to climb straight out of the water. The buffer is the point: cross it and the place empties.

habitatObjects.name: Sheltered Rafting Cove
habitatObjects.description: Calm water in the lee of a point, inside the kelp — flat as a pond even when the swell is running, with fronds lying loose across the surface.

habitatObjects.name: Creosote Bush
habitatObjects.description: The dominant shrub of the Sonoran flats, spaced wide apart because its roots take all the water for metres around. Its resinous leaves smell like rain and lose almost none of it.

habitatObjects.name: Saguaro
habitatObjects.description: A columnar giant that stores months of rain in its pleated stem, swelling and shrinking with the season. Flowers at the crown, fruit in June, and a trunk soft enough to cut into.

habitatObjects.name: Chain-fruit Cholla
habitatObjects.description: A jointed cactus armoured all over in barbed spines that come away at a touch. Inside the tangle of arms is a space almost nothing can push through to.

habitatObjects.name: Desert Mistletoe
habitatObjects.description: A leafless parasitic plant rooted inside mesquite and ironwood branches, hanging in dense green-brown clumps. It fruits in midwinter, when nothing else does.

habitatObjects.name: Chuparosa
habitatObjects.description: A soft grey shrub carrying tubular scarlet flowers right through the desert winter, when almost nothing else is in bloom.

habitatObjects.name: Catclaw Acacia
habitatObjects.description: A low thorny tree of desert washes, hooked all over with curved spines that catch as you pass. Thick cover overhead and heavy seed pods by late summer.

habitatObjects.name: Bush Muhly
habitatObjects.description: A fine-stemmed native perennial grass that grows up through shrubs for protection. It is the first thing livestock graze away, so its return is a sign the flat is healing.

habitatObjects.name: Living Soil Crust
habitatObjects.description: A living skin of cyanobacteria, lichens and mosses knitting the bare soil together. It fixes nitrogen, holds water and blocks weed seedlings — and a single boot or hoof print undoes decades of it.

habitatObjects.name: Open Bare Ground
habitatObjects.description: A patch of soft, uncompacted soil deliberately left open between the shrubs. Loose enough to dig straight down into — but only where nothing has packed it hard.

habitatObjects.name: Harvester Ant Mound
habitatObjects.description: A low gravel-capped mound with a bare cleared disc around it and a rim of discarded seed husks. Whatever is under there moves an astonishing amount of soil.

habitatObjects.name: Buried Deadwood
habitatObjects.description: Dead mesquite and creosote stems worked half into the soil, in contact with damp earth rather than lying dry on the surface. Buried wood breaks down; surface wood just bleaches.

habitatObjects.name: Shrub Litter Mound
habitatObjects.description: Wind-drifted leaves, stems and seed husks caught and heaped under a shrub. Dry and crackling on top, damp and dark underneath after any rain.

habitatObjects.name: Crumbled Soil
habitatObjects.description: Soil laced with fine old galleries and sheeted over with cemented litter, worked through from below rather than from the surface. The tunnels let rain soak in instead of running off.

habitatObjects.name: Tortoise Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A long, cool, straight-sided den dug back into a bank and kept open by use. Far deeper than anything else out here manages, and steady in temperature all year.

habitatObjects.name: Caliche Den
habitatObjects.description: A hollow eroded into a hard caliche bank on a rocky slope — a ready-made chamber with a solid roof, and no digging required.

habitatObjects.name: Creosote Coppice Mound
habitatObjects.description: Wind-caught soil heaped up around a creosote's base and riddled with fine tunnels. The earth is loose and easy to work, and the shrub above hides the doorways.

habitatObjects.name: Seed Larder Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A shallow burrow under a shrub with side chambers packed full of seeds, its entrances plugged with sand every dawn. The plug traps humid air inside, which matters as much as the food does.

habitatObjects.name: Deep Sand Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A spiral shaft driven as much as two and a half metres down into loose soil. At that depth the heat and the dryness of the surface simply do not reach.

habitatObjects.name: Sandy Den
habitatObjects.description: A cool den with several entrances, widened out of an older tunnel rather than dug from scratch. The extra doors are escape routes.

habitatObjects.name: Wash Bank Den
habitatObjects.description: An earthen den dug into the cut bank of a dry wash, set above the flood line — shaded, well-drained, and dry even when the wash runs.

habitatObjects.name: Winter Rock Den
habitatObjects.description: A deep rock fissure running below the frost line that stays above freezing all winter. The same fissure gets used again year after year, sometimes for decades.

habitatObjects.name: Cactus Hollow
habitatObjects.description: The hard, waterproof scar a cactus grows around a hole cut into its trunk — a smooth-walled flask of dried callus. It outlasts the soft flesh around it entirely.

habitatObjects.name: Thorn Thicket Nest
habitatObjects.description: A bulky stick platform wedged a metre or two up inside a thorny shrub. High enough to be off the ground, and prickly enough that nothing follows.

habitatObjects.name: Carrion Ground
habitatObjects.description: An animal that has died, left where it fell instead of hauled away. Within a few days almost nothing is left of it, and all of it is back in the soil.

habitatObjects.name: Saguaro Fruit Fall
habitatObjects.description: Split crimson saguaro fruit at the height of the June heat, just before the rains. For a few weeks it is the richest food and the wettest drink in the whole desert.

habitatObjects.name: Cactus Fruit Set
habitatObjects.description: Prickly pear and cholla hanging heavy with ripe fruit. A crop this size only sets where every flower was properly pollinated first — and out here that is never guaranteed.

habitatObjects.name: Shade Form
habitatObjects.description: A shallow scrape hollowed out in the deep shade under a shrub, down to cool soil. Ten degrees cooler than the open ground a metre away.

habitatObjects.name: Browse Exclosure
habitatObjects.description: A low fence ringed around a patch of oak seedlings. Where browsing pressure is heavy, young oaks never get past knee height — inside the fence, acorns get to become trees.

habitatObjects.name: Nurse Log Seedbed
habitatObjects.description: A rotting, moss-covered log lying on the forest floor. Hemlock seeds that land on bare leaf litter almost always fail; the ones that land on rotten wood become the next generation of trees.

habitatObjects.name: Deep Leaf Mould
habitatObjects.description: Years of undisturbed leaf mould, never raked and never driven over, threaded through with tree roots and fungal strands. This is where the forest's fungi actually live.

habitatObjects.name: Truffle Patch
habitatObjects.description: Underground fungal tubers clustered on oak and hemlock roots. Nothing shows above ground at all; the whole crop sits an inch or two down and has to be smelled out.

habitatObjects.name: Rotting Dead Tree
habitatObjects.description: A small dead stub whose wood has gone soft and pale with white rot, easy to press a thumbnail into. The fungi got here first, and that is what makes it workable.

habitatObjects.name: Rotted-Out Log
habitatObjects.description: A log rotted hollow right through the middle while its outer shell still holds. Inside it is dark, damp and sealed off from the weather.

habitatObjects.name: Downy Woodpecker Hole
habitatObjects.description: A round hole about the width of a thumb, chiselled into a dead trunk and left after a single season. Small, dry, and already made.

habitatObjects.name: Tall Hollow Tree
habitatObjects.description: A large snag carrying a deep rectangular cavity cut into it last spring, big enough to put an arm into. A fresh one gets cut every year, and the old ones stay.

habitatObjects.name: Dead Tree Over Water
habitatObjects.description: A dead trunk standing in shallow water with an old cavity high in it. Nothing below the hole but open air, and several metres down, water.

habitatObjects.name: Peeling Bark Tree
habitatObjects.description: A dying tree whose bark has pulled away from the trunk in loose curling slabs. Behind each slab is a warm, dry, flat gap barely wider than a finger.

habitatObjects.name: Leaf Drey
habitatObjects.description: A ball of leaves and twigs the size of a football, wedged tight into a high fork and woven from the inside out. Rebuilt every year, and rarely left standing empty for long.

habitatObjects.name: Larder Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A burrow entrance no wider than a coin, with tunnels running metres underground to a nest chamber and a storage room holding more than a litre of seeds.

habitatObjects.name: Hemlock Stand
habitatObjects.description: A close-grown group of hemlocks. The canopy holds the snow off the ground beneath it, the shade keeps the stream running cold, and the inner bark stays reachable all winter.

habitatObjects.name: Browse Thicket
habitatObjects.description: Dense young regrowth crowding a gap where a big tree came down — every twig within reach from the ground. It only stays this thick while the browsing pressure stays light.

habitatObjects.name: Crayfish Shallows
habitatObjects.description: A stony, ankle-deep margin of loose flat rocks over gravel, with dark backed-up gaps underneath every one of them.

habitatObjects.name: Root-Mass Den
habitatObjects.description: The dry hollow left under the tipped-up root plate of a fallen tree — roofed with earth and roots, and sheltered from every direction but one.

habitatObjects.name: Earth Den Bank
habitatObjects.description: A well-drained slope with a den dug back into it and several entrances along the face. Enlarged and reused for generations rather than dug fresh.

habitatObjects.name: Forest Winter Den
habitatObjects.description: A deep, rubble-filled crack running below the frost line and staying there all winter. Cold but never freezing, right through to spring.

habitatObjects.name: Broken-Top Chimney Tree
habitatObjects.description: A big living tree snapped off high and hollowed downward by heart rot, leaving an open chimney a foot across. Nothing cuts a cavity this size — it only appears in a tree old enough to rot from the inside.

habitatObjects.name: Hollow Denning Tree
habitatObjects.description: A living tree with a rot-hollowed chamber high in the trunk, dry inside and metres above the forest floor. Nothing that hunts on the ground gets up to it.

habitatObjects.name: Rocky Den Ledge
habitatObjects.description: A dry gap under a leaning slab of rock, screened by brush and open at both ends. Sheltered, but easy to slip out of at the first sound.

habitatObjects.name: Adopted Stick Nest
habitatObjects.description: A bulky old platform of sticks and leaves left behind in a high fork, weathered and a little sagging but still sound. Second-hand, and ready to use in the middle of winter.

habitatObjects.name: Bare Soil Scrape
habitatObjects.description: A hand-cleared patch of open mineral soil, raked back to bare ground. Bare ground is habitat too — seedlings and open earth both need somewhere that isn't covered.

habitatObjects.name: Native Thistle Stand
habitatObjects.description: Wavyleaf thistle, a native prairie thistle rather than one of the invasive European kinds. Deep tubular flowers, and seed heads that break open into soft down.

habitatObjects.name: Grass Thatch Litter
habitatObjects.description: A deep mat of dead grass stems, leaves and roots left where they fell. This is the raw material meadow fungi take apart and hand back to the soil as minerals.

habitatObjects.name: Egg Pod Bank
habitatObjects.description: A strip of firm, sun-warmed bare soil along the edge of the grass, packed hard enough to hold a drilled hole open. Whatever gets buried in it sits out the whole winter there.

habitatObjects.name: Grass Runways
habitatObjects.description: Narrow runways clipped through dense grass at ground level, linking burrow openings and grass-lined chambers. A whole map of little highways hidden under the thatch.

habitatObjects.name: Milkweed Bed
habitatObjects.description: A spreading bed of showy milkweed grown from rhizome cuttings, its stems bleeding white sap wherever they break. Nothing else in the meadow substitutes for it, and one bed slowly becomes a patch.

habitatObjects.name: Nesting Tussock
habitatObjects.description: A dense unmown grass tussock sitting over an abandoned hole in the turf — warm, fur-lined, dry and completely hidden from above.

habitatObjects.name: Brush Hollow
habitatObjects.description: A shallow scrape pressed into the grass under low brush, just deep enough to sit level with the ground. A resting place rather than a burrow — no digging involved.

habitatObjects.name: Berry Thicket
habitatObjects.description: Saskatoon serviceberry, a native shrub with soft twigs and fat buds that stay reachable above the snow, and heavy purple fruit by late summer.

habitatObjects.name: Sap-Rich Stems
habitatObjects.description: Bright orange oleander aphids packed shoulder to shoulder along milkweed stems, thick enough to hide the green underneath. Not a problem to be sprayed — a stand of milkweed carries them every year and is none the worse for it.

habitatObjects.name: Burrow Town
habitatObjects.description: A multi-entrance burrow system dug into deep open soil, its mounded doorways scattered right across a wide patch of ground. Long after it is abandoned the tunnels stay open.

habitatObjects.name: Egg-Case Stem
habitatObjects.description: Stiff dead forb stems left standing through the winter, with a hardened tan foam case glued around one of them. Cut the stems back in autumn and you cut out what is inside them.

habitatObjects.name: Domed Grass Nest
habitatObjects.description: A grass-roofed nest cup woven down into deep bunchgrass, with a covered runway leading in. Only a real expanse of native grass is thick enough to hide one.

habitatObjects.name: Bluebird Nest Box
habitatObjects.description: A wooden box with a small round entrance hole and a metal baffle on the pole below it, facing open grass. The hole is cut to one exact width, and that width is the whole design.

habitatObjects.name: Meadow Winter Den
habitatObjects.description: A rock-and-soil chamber dug below the frost line, often started from an old tunnel in the bank. Room enough down there for a great many bodies at once.

habitatObjects.name: Deep Soil Bank
habitatObjects.description: A bank of deep, stone-free, uncompacted loam — no rock, no hardpan, nothing to hit. Soil like this can be dug faster than it can be walked over.

habitatObjects.name: Earth Den
habitatObjects.description: A south-facing bank widened into a den with several exits, enlarged from an older burrow rather than dug from scratch. Dry, warm early in the year, and quick to leave from.

habitatObjects.name: Crown Stick Eyrie
habitatObjects.description: A bulky platform of sticks wedged into the crown of the tallest tree, with a clear view out over open grass. Built once, then added to and handed on.

habitatObjects.name: Sunlit Mudflat
habitatObjects.description: A bare shelf of wet, sun-warmed mud at the water's edge. Cattail seed is tiny and needs light and open ground to germinate — it will not sprout in shade or under standing water.

habitatObjects.name: Clearwater Shallows
habitatObjects.description: Slow water with the silt settled out of it, so sunlight reaches the bottom. Submerged plants live on that light — which is why clear water and underwater meadows always arrive together.

habitatObjects.name: Litter Drift
habitatObjects.description: A submerged raft of dead cattail and sedge leaves, softening under a fur of fungi and bacteria. More energy moves through a marsh this way — as dead plants — than through anything eaten alive.

habitatObjects.name: Crayfish Burrow Bank
habitatObjects.description: A saturated clay bank riddled with finger-wide tunnels running back into the wet clay. Each one holds water even when the marsh draws right down in late summer.

habitatObjects.name: Submerged Spawning Slab
habitatObjects.description: A flat stone or plank lying just below the surface with a clear gap underneath. The underside is smooth, shaded and scrubbed clean — a ceiling rather than a floor.

habitatObjects.name: Stable Silt Shoal
habitatObjects.description: A broad shelf of settled silt and fine sand in water slow enough that it stays put for years at a time. Soft enough to sink into, stable enough not to shift.

habitatObjects.name: Cattail Root Shallows
habitatObjects.description: Shallow water over a dense mat of cattail rootstocks — starchy, swollen and packed down into the mud. Reachable from underneath even when the surface is frozen over.

habitatObjects.name: Flooded Reed Clump
habitatObjects.description: A tight stand of cattail and reed stems standing in ankle-deep water, stiff enough to hold a weight slung between them. The water underneath is what makes it safe.

habitatObjects.name: Winter Litter Mound
habitatObjects.description: A deep pile of damp leaves, loose bark and old stems heaped on dry ground beside the marsh. Deep enough that the middle of it never quite reaches the temperature of the air.

habitatObjects.name: Fishless Vernal Pool
habitatObjects.description: A shallow, separate pool that fills with snowmelt and dries out completely by late summer. Drying is the point: nothing that needs water year-round can ever establish in it.

habitatObjects.name: Wet Meadow Edge
habitatObjects.description: A band of damp, grassy meadow between the marsh and dry land — never flooded, never properly dry. Lose this band and the marsh ends in a hard edge.

habitatObjects.name: Sandy Nest Bank
habitatObjects.description: A warm, well-drained rise of sand and fine gravel above the waterline, loose enough to dig and quick to drain. Banks like this are far scarcer than they look.

habitatObjects.name: Crane Nest Mound
habitatObjects.description: A broad heap of piled marsh plants built up in open shallow water, its top standing well clear of the waterline. Anything approaching it has to wade.

habitatObjects.name: Hidden Reed Platform
habitatObjects.description: A low platform of living reeds bent down and woven together deep inside a dense stand, barely a hand's width above the water. Invisible from every direction, including above.

habitatObjects.name: Cut Bank Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A bare, vertical earth bank rising straight out of the water, soft enough to tunnel a metre back into and firm enough that the tunnel holds.

habitatObjects.name: Overwater Thicket
habitatObjects.description: Low willow and alder leaning right out over deep still water, their branches hanging a metre above the surface with cool shade underneath.

habitatObjects.name: Old Bank Den
habitatObjects.description: An abandoned bank burrow with its entrance below the waterline and its chamber dry above it. Someone else dug it, and it has stood empty since.

habitatObjects.name: River Bank Den
habitatObjects.description: A roomy den in the bank with an underwater entrance and a dry chamber above — almost always an older lodge or burrow taken over rather than dug fresh.

habitatObjects.name: Dammed Pond
habitatObjects.description: Deep, permanent water held back behind a stick-and-mud dam, with drowned trees still standing in it. Quite different from open cattail marsh — deeper, more open, and it does not appear on its own.

habitatObjects.name: Dug Channel
habitatObjects.description: A shallow dug channel running out from the pond into the marsh, just deep enough to float a branch down. It keeps open water connected right through a dry summer.

habitatObjects.name: Crumbling Log
habitatObjects.description: A soft, damp, half-rotted log going back to soil, crumbling apart when you lift it. Under it the air stays wet all day, whatever the weather is doing above.

habitatObjects.name: Web Anchor Stems
habitatObjects.description: Tall dry stems left standing in a sunny gap, stiff enough to hold a line of silk taut between them.

habitatObjects.name: Maternity Roost
habitatObjects.description: A narrow, dark crevice high off the ground with full sun on the rock outside it. Warm right through the day, and tight enough that anything inside is pressed against the walls.

habitatObjects.name: Barn Loft
habitatObjects.description: A deep wooden box mounted high under a gable, open on one side, with a lip of straw across the sill. Dark and dry inside, well above the ground.

habitatObjects.name: Den Bank
habitatObjects.description: A den dug into a brushy bank, usually an old hole widened out rather than started fresh. Used hard for a few weeks and then left behind.

habitatObjects.name: Damp Leaf Corner
habitatObjects.description: A shaded corner where fallen leaves are left to pile up and soften instead of being cleared away. Underneath it stays damp even through a dry week.

habitatObjects.name: Goat Cliff Ledge
habitatObjects.description: A narrow shelf cut across a near-vertical face, scraped bare and dusty and no wider than a doormat. Ground far steeper than anything else would attempt.

habitatObjects.name: Mineral Lick
habitatObjects.description: A damp bank of salty earth, gnawed and licked down into a hollow. The minerals in it are not in the spring grass, and there is nowhere else this high to get them.

habitatObjects.name: Deep Snow Den
habitatObjects.description: A tunnel driven metres down into a drift that holds into late spring, threaded around fallen boulders, with frozen food stashed in side chambers. A nursery and a freezer at once — and it only works where the snow lasts.

habitatObjects.name: Deep Canyon Edge
habitatObjects.description: The place where the seafloor stops and falls away into cold blue-black depth. Deep water, right up hard against the coast.

habitatObjects.name: Breaking Surf Line
habitatObjects.description: A clean line of waves standing up and toppling along an open beach — a moving wall of white water running the whole length of the shore.

habitatObjects.name: Turtle Grazing Lawn
habitatObjects.description: A patch of eelgrass cropped short and kept that way, its blades staying young and tender instead of growing long and tough. The cropping is what maintains it.

habitatObjects.name: Cactus Crown Nest
habitatObjects.description: A bulky stick platform wedged into the crook where a tall cactus splits into arms — wide enough to stand a whole family on, with a wall of spines below that nothing can climb.

habitatObjects.name: Silk-Lined Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A thumb-wide hole in firm ground, its rim smoothed and bound with silk, and a few trip-lines fanned out across the sand around it. Whatever made it may keep the same one for twenty years.

habitatObjects.name: Elk Wallow
habitatObjects.description: A churned muddy hollow in a forest opening, kept wet and bare by something heavy rolling in it. The puddle left in the dish afterwards holds water for weeks.

habitatObjects.name: Bramble Ground Nest
habitatObjects.description: A grass-lined cup sunk level with the leaf litter beneath an arching bramble. Nothing above it but thorns, and that is the entire defence.

habitatObjects.name: Eagle Nest Crown
habitatObjects.description: The crown of the tallest living tree on the marsh, holding a stick nest the size of a bathtub. A pair returns to the same nest year after year and adds to it until the branch underneath finally gives way.

habitatObjects.name: Still Water Cove
habitatObjects.description: A pocket of open water tucked in behind the reeds where the wind never reaches, its surface as smooth as glass with a few floating stems drifting on it. Nothing disturbs the skin of it at all.

habitatObjects.name: Winter Sleep Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A tunnel driven in under a tilted slab to a grass-lined chamber below the frost line. No larder, no side rooms — just somewhere to lie still, barely above freezing, until spring.

habitatObjects.name: Rock Crack
habitatObjects.description: A dark slot under a loose scree slab, cool, windless and dry, running back further than the daylight reaches. The day's heat never gets to the back of it.

habitatObjects.name: Cliff Seam
habitatObjects.description: A narrow vertical crack running up a sheer rock face, far too tight for anything with proper feet to stand in. The only way in is head-first, and the only way out is a drop.

habitatObjects.name: Wild Grape Tangle
habitatObjects.description: A woody vine roped up a leaning trunk, heavy with fruit by late summer. A ladder and a larder at once — climbable the whole way up, with food waiting at the top.

habitatObjects.name: Snake Egg Mound
habitatObjects.description: A heap of rotting wood chips and bark banked up against a cut stump. It runs warm inside as it rots, which is the whole point — bury something in it and the heap does the work.

habitatObjects.name: Willow Thicket
habitatObjects.description: A damp hollow behind the dunes filled with low willow and bramble, tangled right down to the ground. Nothing of any size can push into it.

habitatObjects.name: Canyon Ledge Den
habitatObjects.description: A dry overhang cut back into a canyon wall and screened by fallen slabs — shaded all day, invisible from below, and reachable by only one route.

habitatObjects.name: Puffball Ring
habitatObjects.description: A ring of pale domes pushing up through old turf. Step on a ripe one and it smokes.

habitatObjects.name: Meadow Sedge Tussock
habitatObjects.description: A dense knee-high clump of sedge in a damp low spot, packed so tightly you could push a fist deep inside it and never find the hole again.

habitatObjects.name: Hidden Grass Nest
habitatObjects.description: A thick tussock left standing in a damp hollow, with the middle pressed down into a deep cup you would walk past without seeing.

habitatObjects.name: Cocoon Leaf Drift
habitatObjects.description: A drift of curled fallen leaves left banked against a log. Giant silk moths spin their cocoons inside a leaf that then falls with it, so the whole next generation is lying in this pile all winter.

habitatObjects.name: Acorn Cache
habitatObjects.description: A patch of soft open ground pocked with little digs where a jay has pushed acorns in one at a time. Most get eaten over winter; the forgotten ones come up as oak seedlings in spring.

habitatObjects.name: Frozen Leaf Bed
habitatObjects.description: A shallow bed of loose leaves and duff over soft soil — only a few centimetres deep, which is all a wood frog needs, because it does not dig below the frost. It simply freezes with the ground and thaws out in spring.

habitatObjects.name: Canopy Nest Limb
habitatObjects.description: A heavy horizontal limb against the trunk of an old tree, high up where the canopy closes over. Big forest hawks need a limb thick enough to hold a nest they will use for years, and clear flying room underneath it.

habitatObjects.name: Thicket Bed Hollow
habitatObjects.description: A scooped, dusty hollow under dense thornscrub where a whole herd lies up through the heat of the day, pressed together. The shade is worth more than the cover — it is ten degrees cooler in there.

habitatObjects.name: Scrape Ledge
habitatObjects.description: A gravel-floored shelf high on a cliff with a shallow dip kicked into the grit. No nest is built here and none is needed — the ledge and the drop below it are the whole thing.

habitatObjects.name: Den Scrap Pile
habitatObjects.description: A dark crevice under a boulder with a rock dragged part-way across the entrance, and a tidy heap of emptied crab shells and drilled clams outside it. The rubbish pile is how you find the octopus.

habitatObjects.name: Meadow Mushroom Ring
habitatObjects.description: A curved arc of pale button caps pushing up through damp grass thatch after rain. The ring is the edge of a fungus growing outward underground, and it can be older than every plant around it.

habitatObjects.name: Bracket Fungus Shelf
habitatObjects.description: Overlapping fans of banded bracket fungus stepping up the side of a dead hardwood log. This is the thing actually digesting the wood — the log only becomes soil because the fungus gets there first.

habitatObjects.name: Wild Celery Bed
habitatObjects.description: Long ribbon leaves streaming underwater in the shallows, rooted in the silt. It lives entirely on the light that reaches the bottom, so it only grows where the water has been allowed to settle clear.

habitatObjects.name: Snowbank Mushrooms
habitatObjects.description: A crowd of small pale mushrooms with hairy stems, fruiting right at the edge of a melting drift on buried rotten conifer wood. They come up while there is still snow on the ground.

habitatObjects.name: Dig Slope
habitatObjects.description: A high bank of loose, root-threaded earth soft enough to be torn open, with the turned soil left in heaps.

habitatObjects.name: Lined Rock Crack
habitatObjects.description: A narrow dry fissure in a wind-scoured rock face, packed at the back with down and fur.

habitatObjects.name: Borrowed Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A burrow mouth someone else dug, widened and swept clean, with a fan of loose sand at the entrance.

habitatObjects.name: Browsed Shallows
habitatObjects.description: A soft-bottomed margin where the water is chest-deep and thick with stems, cropped short in ragged patches.

habitatObjects.name: Splash Ledge
habitatObjects.description: A wet shelf tucked behind a thread of falling meltwater, mossy and permanently in shadow.

habitatObjects.name: Digging Ground
habitatObjects.description: A patch of soft leaf-mould soil left unpacked, already pitted with small cone-shaped holes where something has been turning it over.

habitatObjects.name: Clifftop Burrow
habitatObjects.description: A round hole driven back into deep turf at the very top of a sea cliff, with a worn patch of bare earth at the entrance.

habitatObjects.name: Meadow Burrow Mound
habitatObjects.description: A fan of freshly turned earth banked around a round hole, with a second hole hidden in the grass a few paces off.

habitatObjects.name: Den Hollow
habitatObjects.description: A dry cavity under a leaning log, floored with dragged-in leaves and open at both ends.

habitatObjects.name: Stick Nest
habitatObjects.description: A bulky platform of salt-bleached sticks wedged in a high fork, added to and patched every season.

habitatObjects.name: Happy Buddha
habitatObjects.description: A round little figure sat cross-legged with both arms thrown up and a grin across its whole face. Rubbing the belly is supposed to be lucky, and the clay has gone smooth and shiny in that one spot.

habitatObjects.name: Lucky Toad
habitatObjects.description: A fat three-legged toad sitting on a little heap of coins with one more held in its mouth. Tradition says it faces into the camp, never out, so the luck comes in with you.

habitatObjects.name: Rippled Sand
habitatObjects.description: Clean sand below the low tide line, combed into even ridges by a current gentle enough to leave them standing.

habitatObjects.name: Bunchgrass Sod Plug
habitatObjects.description: A hand-cut plug of native bunchgrass, roots and soil together. Set it in bare ground and it spreads on its own.

habitatObjects.name: Meadow Overlook Bench
habitatObjects.description: A second bench, set at the far edge of the meadow facing back the way you came. Best an hour before dusk, when the grass goes gold and the bees are still up.

habitatObjects.name: Pollinator Waystation
habitatObjects.description: A raised bed of nectar plants set deliberately in the open, halfway between two flowering patches, so a short-range bee can cross ground it otherwise could not.

habitatObjects.name: Meadow Lantern Row
habitatObjects.description: Lanterns strung low along a path on a woven cord. Hung at knee height on purpose — high lights wash out the meadow and the moths never settle.

habitatObjects.name: Forest Reading Bench
habitatObjects.description: A plank bench gone soft green along its north edge. The moss is not neglect; it is the only thing here that will not give you splinters.

habitatObjects.name: Hollow Trail Marker
habitatObjects.description: A carved marker for the paths through the deep stand, where every direction is the same brown column and you have already been wrong once.

habitatObjects.name: Old Hollow Arch
habitatObjects.description: A bent-branch arch at the mouth of the oldest trees. It marks nothing, holds nothing up, and everyone slows down walking under it anyway.

habitatObjects.name: Reed Weaver's Bench
habitatObjects.description: A low bench with a reed-woven seat, set back far enough from the water that a heron will still work the shallows in front of you.

habitatObjects.name: Rushwater Boardwalk Rail
habitatObjects.description: A railed run of boardwalk over soft ground. The rail is the point: it keeps feet on the planks, and marsh that nobody walks on knits back together fast.

habitatObjects.name: Heron Watch Arch
habitatObjects.description: A reed-bound arch framing the open water. Stand under it and stay still; herons mind a moving outline far more than a standing one.

habitatObjects.name: Shade Ramada
habitatObjects.description: An open-sided roof on posts, no walls. Walls would trap the afternoon heat; a roof and a through-breeze drop the ground beneath it by a startling amount.

habitatObjects.name: Redstone Waymarker
habitatObjects.description: A stacked marker on the ridge line, sited to be visible from the wash below — where the walls are high, the sun is overhead, and every bend looks like the last.

habitatObjects.name: Geode Sun Court
habitatObjects.description: A ring of split geodes set crystal-face up around a swept floor. At noon the whole court throws light back at you; at dusk it goes quiet and violet.

habitatObjects.name: Graywind Rest Bench
habitatObjects.description: A stone bench in the lee of the ridge, put where the wind is not. Ten steps either side and you would not be able to hear yourself think.

habitatObjects.name: Lichen Cairn Trail
habitatObjects.description: A line of cairns for the stretch above the last trees. Built tall on purpose: the ones that matter are the ones still showing after snow.

habitatObjects.name: Summit Sundial
habitatObjects.description: A quartz gnomon on a stone plate. Runs fast in summer and is useless in cloud, which up here is most of the interesting weather.

habitatObjects.name: Driftwood Bench
habitatObjects.description: A bench built from what the winter storms delivered, set above the wrack line so the next winter has to work harder to take it back.

habitatObjects.name: Shore Waymark
habitatObjects.description: A driftwood post with a sea-glass eye set into the head. It catches the low sun and tells you where the path leaves the sand.

habitatObjects.name: Tidewatcher's Arch
habitatObjects.description: Two storm-cured trunks leaned into an arch above the high-tide line. Twice a day the water comes almost to the feet of it, and twice a day it does not.

tools.name: Gathering Basket
tools.description: For gently collecting light, renewable materials: seeds, berries, flowers, fiber, shells.

tiers.name: Gathering Basket
tiers.effect: Carry up to 200 materials and gather 1 at a time.

tiers.name: Reinforced Gathering Basket
